ROME, Dec. 15.-Italian labor
threw another sharp strike punch
today in its running battle for
higher pay. Millions of indus
trial, construction and utilities
workers walked of their jobs
for "a hours.


It was the second nation wide
strike in five days and the third
of the fall and winter. The
walkouts are held to "a hours
because neither the workers nor
their unions have the money for
a long strike.


Construction projects in Rome
were idle but some factory work.
ers in the capital and in the
industrial north reported for
work. In Genoa, a government
spokesman said most industries
along the Ligurian Coast includ-
ing the nations largest shipyardS
were idle.


Phone Calls Go Through.


Despite union orders, many
employees of privately owned tele-
phone systems reported for work.
Long distance calls went through
without hitch.


Water, gas and electric serv-
ices and bread and milk deliv-
cries were maintained.


Last Friday about a million
Government employees. including
railroad and postal workers.
struck for a day. An estimated
| 7 million workers walked out
September Is in a 24-hour show
of strength.


Third Union Balks.
Italy's biggest union, the Com
munist-bossed General Confed-
Grafton Of Labor. and the anti
Red Free Confederation Of La
bor called the walkout today.
A third large organization, the
Italian Labor Union, said the
strike just before Christmas was
badly timed and refused to par
ticipate.


All the unions are pressing
for changes in Italy's compli-
Gated wage structure to boost
the workers total pay.


The industrial federations are
fighting the change, contending
it would add 10 per cent to their
total labor bill. The unions say
it would add only 4 per cent.

east of here.

farm home.

quick medical examination dis
closed Emma was not harmed,
except for scratches.


The girl was wearing only
boomers when she was last seen.
They soon were torn off as she
wandered through almost i'm
penetrable wilderness.


ITS a wonder that she is
alive" commented Pfc. Anthony
Cywinski, one Of the State police
officers who rushed the child to
a hospital. "She was only 2
miles away from home at the
most, but how she got that far
in these terrible forests I'll never
know"

FORESTVILLE, Quebec, Aug.
20.-Provincial police searched
today for evidence of arson in
the two forest fires which burned
more than 165 square miles of
timberland near here before
being checked.


Two men are being held under
guard as important" witnesses,
and Investigations are continu-
ing, police said.


The main blaze, which started
August 7. has swept no farther
in the last SO hours, due partly
to a shift in wind and damp,
cool weather. Some 800 fire.
fighters had chance to enlarge
f1re-breaks around the threat
ened communities of Sainte
Therese and Canton Latour.


A smaller fire, spotted Mon
day near Sainte Therese, has
been confined to an area of
about l square mile.


Authorities said the fires
would need close watching for
some time but only high winds
would now endanger Sainte
Therese and Canton Latour.

Women fear above all things
old age. For with it comes
wrinkles, brittle bones, faltering
steps and a querulous attitude
toward life. But, there are wom-
en- who seem to grow younger
with the years-they are ageless!
They do not fold their hands
simply looking forward to the end
but with each day find things to
employ their minds that time
shall not hang heavy on their
hands. Another thing, the age
less especially women" never
retire at night without getting
rid of the dust and CRIME, also
the cares of the day. Cleansing
the face and body assures one
of lovelier tomorrow and for.
getting the harassments of the
working hours gives passage into
a peaceful and refreshing night
of dreams in which the lines of
care are erased and sleep lays
its healing hand upon the tired
brow. Selah!

ism.


In an overwhelming vote of
confidence in Premier David
Ben-Gurion, the Israeli Parlia-
ment last night approved, 1916,
q government statement reject
ing these reasons for severing
diplomatic ties.

GRAND CANYON, Ariz., May
30.-The mystery of the para
chutes which dropped into Grand
Canyons darkened depths ap-
parently will remain unsolved.


Sheer cliffs and lodges forced
back a team Of rangers today,
and the Air Force refused to
send a helicopter into the
treacherous chasm, where air
currents might dash the craft.


Air Force spokesman said they
had no evidence that the para
chutes had held any one, and
that no planes were reported
missing. The chutes dropped
mysteriously from the sky late
Thursday.


Maj. William Casterline, base
operations officer at Luke Air
Force Base, said he felt the
chutes probably carried instru-
ments to test weather or radar
equipment.

Christmas lift for servicemen

The Crucial Moment.


When the pilots at Moses
Lake cranked off their engines
they had $4,000 horse power
behind them. The crucial mo-
ment came when the big plane
wheeled away from its parking
place on the ramp.


At this point, the pilot and
co-pilot. running through their
check list are supposed to make
certain that the gust locks have
been released. These are the
locks which hold the ailerons.
rudder and elevators rigid so
that they cannot be damaged
by wind while the plane is on
the ground.


The lever releasing these locks
also releases the throttle for
take-off power when desired,
The device was designed as a
double safety check. In theory.
the pilot would not be able to
get take-off power until the
locks on the control surfaces had
been fully released.


1t was brought out later, how
ever, that the first downward
movement of the lever released
the throttles. If for some reason
the lever was not moved into the
full downward position, the pilot
could obtain full power and at
least partial control of the al
leronS and tail surfaces.


Pilot Can't See Lever.


The lever in question can nei-
ther be seen nor reached by the
first pilot. The co-pilot orders
another crew member to throw
the dual release while going over
the pre-takeoff check list with
the airplane commander.


Normal procedure for the first
pilot is to move his controls to
test their freedom of action after
hearing the order for release of
the gust locks. House members

fact the locks were not fully re-
leased.

shortly after noon.

ing for withdrawal of foreign
troops from embattled Korea-a
familiar Communist chant-and
opposed sending Japanese troops
to Korea" No responsible Jap
anese official has ever suggested
sending japanese to Korea.


They also opposed "the Japan
Republic of Korea agreement"
Japan and South Korea have not
even begun talks designed to
lead to a diplomatic agreement
and will not do so for some time.


The pickets said they repre-
Sented the National Unification
League and were from all parts
of Japan.


A group of 20 conferred with
an American Embassy official,
but the Embassy would not say

inal lawyers.


Law is unique among the professions.

vania, New York, New Jersey and few other

pixies, State officials have been giving serious
thought to the subject. Favorable action may

which to supply them The volume of traffic
has been increasing in recent years faster than

revenues from gasoline taxes have not kept
pace. AS the financial problem has become more
acute, the idea of collecting tolls to defray the
cost of expensive new limited-acceSs express
ways has grown in favor.


The proposed Richmond Petersburg turn
pike would parallel U. S. /, roughly, for the
35-mile distance. The engineers suggested
two possible routes, one cutting through parts
of the two cities and the other bypasSing them
through rural regions. The former plan was
preferred by the consultants, but special act
of the Legislature would be required. Under
the present law the State Highway Comnis
sion could build a toll road through rural areas
but not through any cities. A legislative COM
mittee also is studying the toll-road plan in

mendations to the next General Assembly. 1t
would not be surprising if Virginia becomes the
next State to adopt the toll system for certain
alternate main routes. Unless this policy
change is made, the State may find itself falling
behind in it's efforts to keep it's fine roads
abreast of rising traffic demands.

The Queen will make her an

and Princess Anne, by means of !

as chairman of the Civil Service
Commission.

uate School of Business Ad-

versity, succeeds Robert Rams

Filling the job was hurry-up

CHICAGO. Jan. 3.-The trend
Of grain prices was downward
throughout 1852. Two words give
the reason: Big crops.


Crops were big in this country
and, equally important, they were
big in some other countries which
compete with the United States
In the world export market. Can
ada had a record-breaking wheat
crop.


Demand was not too brisk. Eu-
fopean countries. probably anxious
70 conserve dollar credits. became
less aggressive buyers of American
wheat than in the previous year
Smaller pig production reduced
that outlet for feed grains, but
beef cattle numbers increased.


Weather Always Big Factor.


The year ended with an uncer-
tain outlook. Weather, as usual.
would be a major factor in this
years grain market-and no one
can predict the weather for a
year ahead with anything resem-
bling certainty.


This years winter wheat crop,
to be harvested in tn spring. was
causing some concern. SubSoil
moisture was not considered good
in the Southwest. But large sup
plies will be carried over into next
year from previous crops. Other
major cereals have not been
planted, but here. too. there are
likely to be large carryovers from
previous crops.


The Agriculture Department has
cautiously predicted, "the overall
level of feed (grain) prices may
not be greatly different from that
of 1951-52."

corn and cash oats all were set in

SEOUL, Jan. 8.-An allied
raiding party stabbed into Chi
nese lines on the western front
today and blasted the Reds with
practically every weapon in their
arsenal.


The raiders struck at dawn
with flame-throwers, tank fire,
artillery anG mortar shells,
soaring jellied gasoline bombs.
air strikes, hand grenades,
satchel charges and small arms
fire.


When the raiders withdrew IS
minutes later they counted IS
Chinese bodies strewn in the
snow east of the Panmunjom
neutral corridor. At least IS
others were believed killed or
wounded.


It was the second slashing raid
by United Nations forces in "a
hours.


Temperature Near Zero.


Skies continued clear today.
The thermometer dipped to 3
degrees on the western front
before dawn. The high reported
along the front yesterday was
barely below freezing.


Last night raiding South Ko-
rean infantrymen and engineers
blew up a tunnel which North
Koreans had been digging into
Anchor Hill, key position of the
far eastern front. They killed
A Reds.


Creeping up the tunnel, the
ROKs killed three entrance
guards and exploded 200 pounds
of INT inside the mouth of the
cave.


Withdrawing after the thun-
derous blast, the ROKs smashed
into a North Korean platoon and
killed five and wounded nine
Reds, bringing the total Red
casualties in that action to 81, a
United States 9th Army spokes-
man said.


Ammunition Blown Up.


Another ROK raiding unit
blew up a forward enemy am
munition dump south of Anchor
Hill. They killed seven North
Koreans in the battle that fol-
lowed.


The rest of the 155-mile
ground front was relatively quiet.


United States Super Forts last
night bombed a rail marshalling
yard and supply center above
Wonsan, Red port city on the
east coast.


One bomber force struck the
supply target between Hamhung
and WonSan, while other Super
Forts hit the rail yard at Ko-
won.


The 5th Air Force reported
more of its warplanes made
strikes on the eastern sector of
the front and against Commu-
mist rail lines near Sariwon,
making some rail cuts and dam
aging two boXcars.


Twin-engined B-26 light
bombers destroyed SIS Commu-
mist trucks last night. the Air
Force said.

BELGRADE, Yugoslavia, April
27.-Yugoslavia's federal execu-
tive council has drafted a new
law spelling out the limits of
religious freedom under Presi-
dent Marshal Tito's Communist
regime.


The law-published yesterday
and certain of parliamentary ap-
proval later this year-reaffirms
the Yugoslav Constitutions basic
guarantee Of freedom of worship.
However, it rejects demands of
the Catholic church. including
those for religious instruction in
public schools and unrestricted
circulation of church papers.
Holds All Religions Equal.
The new law calls specifically
for a separation of schools from
religious instruction and puts
religious literature under the
general laws governing the press,
thus allowing government con-
troll


The law declares as a basic
principle that all religions are
equal and bans discrimination
against individuals on the basis
of religious conviction. It per-
mits religious schools to train
| future clergymen and allows the
clergy to hold services on church
grounds, form their own organl-
cations and collect money for
expenses.


It prohibits the spreading
of anti government material
through religious schools. press
or ceremonies and bans forced
membership in religious organi-
cations. The law declares, also,
that there will be no military
service exemptions for religious
reasons.


Vatican Attacked.


Penalties for violations are Is
days imprisonment or a fine of
10000 dinars ($33).


The special commission which
drafted the new law called in
church leaders for consultations.
but talks with the Catholic
Church broke off after the initial
session last week. The govern
ment charged interference by
the Vatican, with which it has
severed diplomatic relations.


Serbian Orthodox and Moslem
leaders were reported to be in
general accord with the terms of
the draft law.

ORANGE, Tex, Nov. 28.-The
22-year-old love idyll of Betty
McCuddy and Tom Buntin was
shadowed by tragedy today after
their second grandchild, a girl,
was born dead.


Tom and Betty. who became
Mr.. and Mrs. Thomas D. Pal
mer after they disappeared in
1881 from their homes in Nash
vile, Tenn, and Russellville, KY,
had feared it would happen.


Ever since their secret love
became public knowledge Thurs
day they had tried to protect
their pregnant daughter Eliza
beth from the excitement of pub
licity.


Please" Betty. now a court
stenographer. had told reporters,
don't ask me questions now.
Come back in a few days and
I'll talk gladly, but not now."


Ask Time to Think.


"Give us time to think things
over" Tom. a television sales
man. had said.


The man who had been q
prominent Nashville insurance
executive and the pretty young
woman who had been his secre-
tary--both long declared dead
only Thursday emerged as a
happy couple with six children in
this little Gulf Coast refining
center.


In deep gloom after their old
secret became known, they were
surrounded almost Immediately
by friends, neighbors and fellow
churchgoers who sought to re-
assure and protect them. Then
their manners became more
carefree.


Yesterday, Tom decided they
wouldn't talk any more about
their life. That's the attitude
my wife and I'll maintain" he
said. When expectant Elizabeth,
81. was taken to a hospital,
Orange Police Chief Raymond
Sanders asked reporters and
photographers to leave them
alone" But Betty-Mrs. Palmer
agreed to pose for pictures.


Mother Hospitalized.


Then came the tragic still
birth and Mrs. Palmer, bitterly
blaming the publicity of the past
few days, was hospitalized in ex-
treme shock. Elizabeth was re-
ported in good condition.


Elizabeth is the wife of Ma
rine Corpl. William Burton in

which well-wishers had filled
with flowers in the past two
days.


The Nashville TenneSsean, in

BERLIN, Aug. 2S.-West Ger
man police using batons and
water hoses last night broke up
demonstrations by 5000 Com
munists trying to impede the
distribution of American donated
food to East Germans.


The Communist rowdies failed
to prevent 10000 hungry East
Germans from collecting their
food parcels as the relief pro-
gram went into high gear after
an 11-day showdown for reor-
ganization


The Red demonstrators ap-
peared at two points of the
inter-sector border, yelling Slo-
gans and threatening the people
waiting for the parcels. Sixty
four persons were arrested.


Hoses Rout Reds.


The biggest demonstration was
in the Wedding district of the
French sector where Communists
scattered leaflets attacking the
American food relief plan. On
the British sector border, near
the Tiergarten park, the Com
munists shot over rockets that
rained propaganda leaflets when
they burst.


West German police threw
back the Communists by a play
of water streams from hoses
mounted on revolving turrets
aboard riot squad trucks.


Construction workers on the
East Berlin Stain Alice build
ing project were reported last
night to have threatened a mass
march into West Berlin to get
food parcels if Communist off,
cials don't stop harassing parcel
collectors.


May March Into West


The we'll informed Free Jur-
lists Committee said that the
workers have protested against
Communist threats to fire any
man accepting American food.
They have also decreed that the
guilty would lose their ration
cards.


If these threats are not with
drawn, the men plan to link arms
and march in massed thousands
into the West sectors, East Ger
man sources told the JuriSts'
association.


1t was a similar protest march
against increased work norms
by the Stain Alec workers that
touched off the June II anti
Communist revolt in East Ger
many.


One East German drew a
burst Of eight shots from a Red
policemen's submachine gum as
he dashed into the West sector.


The hordes from the Com
munist zone eagerly snapped up
seven-pound packages contain
ing lard, milk, and -four, at
present unobtainable in their
home towns.


Some arrived the previous
night and slept huddled together
outside the distribution points.
At dawn, more moved into Vest
Berlin. summoned by Western

One of the interesting and potentially
significant sideshows playing on the European
stage these days is that centering around
the long negotiations for new Balkan entente
among Yugoslavia, Greece and Turkey. While
the exact extent and form of eventual agree
ment seemingly has not yet been worked out,
the open exchanges of official visits and the
publicly avowed desires to reach solid UNDER
standing indicate considerable progress.


There are many complications-som Of
historic nature and others Of more current
MISUNDERSTANDING upon the military and
political aspects Of an alliance among these
three nations. The fact that Greece and Turkey
are members of the NATO makes 1t difficult,
II not impossible, for them to sign durable
and all-out military pact with non-member
The fact that Yugoslavia is Communist
country-although at complete odds with Sta
inist communism-poSes an obvious problem
vis-a-vis Communist Greece and Turkey
Beyond these factors however, is the common
denomination of being geographically and ira
ditionally in the path of aggressive Russian
aspirations. Turkey, Greece and Yugoslavia are,
in effect, the front line of defense against
Soviet push into Southern Europe or the Medi-
terranean basin.


Aside from the defensive potential however,
a concord between these three states could have
an even more disturbing effect upon Moscow's
control over such helpless satellites as Bulgaria,
Romania, Hungary and Albania. It would, per-
haps, be overoptimistic to feel that the Soviet
grip on these countries is an uncertain one. BY
their usual tactics of suppression and decima-
ton, the Soviet Communists have taken over
the governments and reshaped the political and
economic lives of these satellites. There are
no such processes. however, by which they can
feel permanently sure that they have obliter-
ated historic opposition to Russian imperialism
or deeply rooted traditions of nationalism.


That the three anti-Soyiet Balkan nations
are aware of the role which they might play
quietly in spreading discomfort among the bor-
dering Iron Curtain countries has been indi-
Gated in the propaganda which has been ema-
mating intermittently, particularly from Bel
grade, toward these nearby captive peoples. It
Is the feeling In the West, and there are good
reasons to accept it within limitation, that
there are "soft spots" behind the Iron Curtain
where a persistent and carefully devised STRAIT
egy Of psychological warfare might create seri-
Gus trouble for the Kremlin conspirators The
satellites within or bordering upon the Balkans
may be included in these vulnerable lands. and
an anti-Soviet Balkan entente may some day
constitute an effective offensive staging area.

ernment House and the residence

relentless allied blows on Red
Korea.

COPENHAGEN, Oct. 27.-A
Soviet torpedo boat hailed the
Danish fishing vessel Villim in
the Baltic Sea off the island of
Gotland, touching off a strange
chase that obviously bewildered
the Russians.


The Danish skipper, Oerge
Finne. told the story today when
he returned to port with a catch
of salmon.


When the Soviets hailed his
craft, Finne, who knows no Rus
sian, assumed he had been cap
tured. He sent a message home
reporting his supposed plight and
dutifully followed the Red war;
ship.


This went on for several hours.
Then Finne noticed the torpedo
boat officers had gathered on the
vessels deck and were staring
at the tiny fishing craft through
their binoculars.


Sensing something was wrong,
Finne stopped his ship - and
nothing happened. The Russians
sailed on their way, apparently
relieved to have gotten rid of
their "purSuer."

British warships attacking"
NATO shipping in vast maneuv-

sailors were reported injured.
none seriously.

British ships was due to rendez-
vouS today with the main body
of the fleet that includes the
United States battleship Iowa
and British, Canadian and
American aircraft carriers
Britain's only battleship in ac-

leading the small British force

World War II.

the SWiftsure had lodged both
air and sea attacks. Earlier this
week, American airmen under
orders to sink" the Swiftsure
mistakenly attacked the Van
guard.


The SwlftSure, armed with a
main battery of nine 6-inch
guns, was completed in 1914.
The Diamond, commissioned in
February, 1852, is one of a class
including the largest fleet de-
stroyers ever built for the Royal
Navy. She carries a peacetime
complement of 308 men.


The Swiftsure was the first
British ship to re-enter Hong

render. The Diamond was the
first navy vessel commissioned
after the death of King George
vi IN February, 1852, and thus
became the first new ship to join
Britain's Navy during the reign
of Queen Elizabeth II.

A consolidated department of

major recommendations of a
proposed Alexandria Govern
ment reorganization plan made
public today.


The plan represents the first
phase in the administrative sur
vey being conducted by the In

City Manager Ira Willard ex-

mended by the surveyors are

Gil and department heads can
study them and make sugges-
tons.


Consolidate Finance Setup.


In their report, the surveyors
give a general outline of de-
partmental organization for the
city. The principal difference
between their outline and the
present municipal setup is a con-
Solidated department of finance,
in charge of all the city's fiscal
function.


Alexandria now has a direc-
tor of finance who prepares
budgets and serves as a con-
troller, but there are three other
Independent observation-disclosures
missioner of revenue, treasurer
and city collector-in charge of
tax collection, assessment and
tax billing.


The report comments that leg
islation would be necessary to
bring all financial functions un-
der one department. This was
proposed in Alexandria several
years ago, but voters rejected
the idea in a referendum.


Office Under City Manager.


The outline provides a new
office under the city manager in
charge of general administra-
ton. The surveyors say it would
be the task of this office to con-
duct work programs and produc-
ton analyses, procedures analy-
SeS, research work and reports
communications, records and leg
islative liaison.


The outline emissions 13 major
departments under the City
Council and city manager. The
city now has 16, excluding the
elective Offices.


Those departments that would
be absorbed within the new plan
are: Assessments, plumbing in
Spection and coming. Five OF
the 13 departments under the
new setup would serve as staff
and management units, directly
under the city manager. These
departments are: City plan
ming, finance, personnel, general
administration and civil defense.


Personnel also would be a new
department, but the city already
has provided funds for it's crea-
ton in this years budget.


The surveyors explained that
the staff and management de-
partment would operate as aides
for the city manager, Analysing
and working out details of rec
concentrations that come from
the operating department.


The eight operating depart.
ments also report directly to the
city manager, but not in the
same advisory capacity as the
staff and management depart.
ment. The eight proposed op-
Grating departments are: Police
traffic and parking, public works
building and coming, fire, health
welfare and recreation.


Go to Technical Aspects.


MI Willard said the surveyor:
now will proceed with more tech.
nical aspects of their study tt
recommend what procedures
personnel, etc., are necessary.

Long ago cities like st. Louis saw to

CASTOR Dominica, gnarled old
mountain farmer who has con-
fessed the triple Staying of an
English family Is months ago,
tried to throw himself over a
railroad bridge today during a
re-enactment of the crime.


Police grabbed the bearded,
76-year-old farmer before he
could carry out his apparent at
tempt at suicide.


Accused by two of his own
sons, the old man was charged
formally today with the Staying
on August S, 1852, of British
nutrition expert Sir Jack Drum
mond, Lady Drummond and
their 11-year-old daughter.


The Drummonds, holidaying
in France, were slain at their
road side camp site 200 yards
from Dominicis stone farm home
near here in Southeastern
France.


Police said the old man broke
down and confessed the killings
after his sons accusations and
48 hours of police grilling.


New Version of Motive.


The French press agency. in
new version of the farmers
alleged confession. said he killed
the Drummonds after Sir Jack
surprised him in an attempt to
attack Lady Drummond.


But Police Commissioner Ed
mond Sebeille denied that Domi-
nici had admitted any attack at
tempt.


Earlier, Detective Georges Har-
zig had told a news conference
that Sir Jack caught the old man
watching Lady Drummond un-
dress.


Sir Jack, 81, had gained fame
in Britain for organizing the
wartime austerity diet which
kept the islanders fit while Ger
man submarines preyed on their
shipping.


Mr.. Harzig gave this version
Of the confession:


The <old man, out. hunting,
walked near the Drummond car.
He went closer to spy on her.
The woman saw or heard him
and screamed, arouSing her hus-
band. The two men quarreled,
traded blows, and Dominica fired.
first at Sir Jack, then at his
wife, killing them both.


Then the old man fired at the
child, Elizabeth. The bullet only
creased her and she ran scream
ing toward the nearby Durance
River. Dominica chased her and
she fell. AS she begged for
mercy, he clubbed her to death
with his rifle stock.


Returned to Scene of Crime.


Dominica, the father of eight
children, was returned to the
scene of the crime today for a
check on his confession. His
dash for the bridge came just
before the re-enactment Of the
crime reached the death of the
child. A police inspector play
ing Elizabeth's role had opened
the car door and run for the
river. .*


Playing his role, Dominica
numbered after but kept on 60

was caught and brought back.
AS the police inspector covered
in feigned terror. Dominica went
through the motions of smash
ing his skull.

patient police investigation
hampered by the hostile silence
of the peasants of this region
of the lower Alps. The first
break came two days ago when
two of Dominici's sons, Gustave
and Clovis, told police their
| father was the killer.

The Reds apparently had over

ing force.

bility that the Wet Mini may

! Luang Prabang, 275 miles south

A Chevy Chase citizens group

park near East-West highway.

Roads Commission, although en-
gineers are known to favor the

through the Chevy Chase area.

purposely left the southeast leg

tercounty belt highway.

B" proposal contend it Is six

cheaper.

long disputed Trieste free ter
ritory."

mentS in the long dispute.


Yugoslavia officially denied
yesterday Italian charges that
that President Tito was getting
ready to annex the territory's
Zone B, south of the port city
which Yugoslavia occupies and
administers under the Italian
peace treaty.


U. S. Support Charged.


Yugoslav Foreign Undersecr0-
tary Ales Bebler also charged
yesterday in a speech at Idrija,
on the Slovene coast, that the
Italians were "endeavoring with
all means available" to annex
the United States-British occu-
pied, Zone A of the territory,
which includes the port.


Bebler asserted that "the Ital-
ians are getting the support of
the Anglo American military
government in Trieste"


United States diplomats in
Rome and Belgrade were report
ed relatively undisturbed over
the increased tension between
Italy and Yugoslavia.


officials in Rome confirmed
that an Italian infantry regi-
ment and an armored battalion
had been deployed along the

the alert. But the officials
termed these actions routine ex-
erciseS' as part of maneuverS
under way in the area for some
time.

Rome newspapers reported,
without official explanation. that
an Italian cruiser, two destroyers
and a number of small vessels
sailed last night into Venice Har-
Dor, across the Northern Adriatic
from Trieste.


Trieste's Italian-language press
echoed Rome's fears at possible
new Yugoslav moves and the
city's political leaders conferred
about the situation. The gen.
eral public, however, remained
unexcited.


Italy's 1947 peace treaty pro-
vided that all Trieste be free
territory under United Nations
supervision but the Western pow
ers and Russia have never been
able to agree on an international
governor. In the absence of this
agreement, the British-American
and Yugoslav occupations of the
two zones have continued.


The Western allies have been
hopeful Tito and the Italians
would reach agreement on Tri-
este in direct negotiations, but
SO far the two neighbors have
not even been able to agree on
bases on which to start talks.

RACINE, Wis, July 11.-Mrs.

her first step when she was only
eight days old.


It happened this way, says
Mrs. Koltyn:


Kelli was born June 81, weigh
ing seven pounds. Eight days
later, lying on her stomach on
the kitchen table waiting for
her bath. the baby skooched
her knees up under her, straight
ened her elbows and pushed.
Mrs. Koltyn caught her daugh-
ter under the chest. Kelli kept
pushing with her feet. And Kelli
was walking. While the aston
ished mother held Kelli's shoul-
ders, the tiny youngster pranced
around the table.


Mrs. Koltyn called DR.. Roland
Schacht. He came, watched and
decided Kelli's trip was most
unusual" Babies are often a
year old before they walk.


While doctors, grandparents
and photographers crowded the
kitchen yesterday, Kelli gave a
repeat performance. She re-
peated her hike while Drs. Ed
mund and Roland Schacht
manned cameras. A newspaper
photographer popped hashbulbs.
Then Kelli yawned and went to
sleep.


Doctors say the baby probably
will keep on walking unless she
develops stage fright.

tempting to take over the gov
ernment by fomenting militant

nation.

rell house had been overlooked

ferred to billing lists.

visorS to waive the penalty.

thetic but unyielding.


'It certainly seems unfair. but

waive the penalty and interest"

NEW YORK, Sept. 1.-THE

for the year today with heavy
selling.

sections of the market. Indivi-

points were frequent. Some

that.


Volume built up swiftly as
prices declined and the high

in April.


The fast pace was at a rate
we'll above yesterdays 100000

down sharply.

bearish. Railroads yesterday

today the industrial segment of

previous bottom. That consti-
tuted a sell signal for many
short term traders. Other SELL
ing soon was brought into the
market.


Railroads, motors and steels
were most active, but utilities,
oils, coppers. distillers, chem
icalS and other major divisions
of the list we're also lower.


The heaviest part of the SELL
ing furry lasted less than Is
minutes at the start of the third
hour. There was a little recov-
cry from the lows when the
burst spent itself.

cents at $102.01, a new low for
the year.

phone, Du Pont, General Elec-
t1c, U. S. Steel, Chrysler, Stude-

week.

guilty plea to smothering and

These are days for a cracking fire and
pleasant moments at the hearth. There is
warmth for more than the body in the flames
of an open fireplace. The man with fireplace
can begin from there to count his blessings.


There are both memories and dreams in the
leaping blaze. The rain and chill wind outside
are far removed, and other realities vanish with
the lighting of the kindling and the nursing OF
the flame The dreams crystalline. The fireplace
closes in and stabilizes the personal world.


The fire on the hearth once was the prin-
cipal source of winter heat, and the house
which possessed fewer than three could barely
be called home. The hungry coal scuttle was
bane of childhood. Or, where wood was plenti-
full, trip into the cold, and sometimes snow,
to replenish the fuel, was made with reluctance.
Cleaning the flue was another bothersome
chore. But when the fire was lit and going, and
the coal scuttles full or the wood piled high,
the fireplace was the center of activity. The
scholar studied there. 1t was there that socks
were darned and magazines and the evening
paper read. The cat slept amicably alongside
the dog.


The fireplace today has the advantage Of
luxury. Toting the wood and cutting the
kindling are part of the ritual and the dis
sension is concerned not with who shall be
forced to do these jobs, but with who shall have
the privilege. brightly burning fire. bowl
of popcorn and an apple or two-that is the
prescription for casting OF todays worries, and
recalling yesterday or dreaming OF tomorrow.
1t is a most palatable medicine.

Two bills authorizing financial
aid to school systems affected by
Federal employment probably
will come to the House floor to-
morrow.


The House Rules Committee
today gave the green light to the
two measures. Majority Leader
Halleck said he hoped to bring
them up for debate tomorrow.


One bill authorizes $273 mil
lion for school construction and
the other $50 million for main
tenance and operation.


Neither bill would aid District
schools, but nearby communities
stand to receive funds if the bills
are approved and followed up by
actual appropriations.


Would Continue Program.


The proposed legislation would
continue Federal programs al
ready in operation.


The construction bill continues
aid in this category only for one
year, but the other bill runs for
two years.


Chairman Mcconnell of the
House Education and Labor
Committee said a study of the
whole future of these programs
is to be made and that his
committee was recommending
the bills as a temporary action
pending completion of the study,
which will take about two years.


Rules Committee members
expressed sympathy with the
type of aid represented in the
two bills, but several members
made it clear they opposed any
aid carrying with it Federal
control of local school systems.
Mr.. Mcconnell said he opposes
any such control too.


Obligation Seen, However.


Mr.. Mcconnell pointed out,
however, that the armed forces
and other Federal agencies have
created serious problems for
many school systems and that
he felt the Federal Government
has an obligation to help meet
those problems.


Arlington, Alexandria and
Fairfax stand to receive some
money under the construction
bill, and area schools probably
would receive more than 81 mil
lion for maintenance and opera
tions purposes. The allotments
are made under a complicated
formula, so the exact amounts
aren't known yet.


The Rules Committee voted to
allow an hours debate on each
bill.

Battle-weary United States Ma
rines pulled of the summit of
bloody outpost Vegas Saturday
night before frantic Chinese Red
attacks and allied artillery began
churning it with constant ex-
plosions.


It was the third time since
Thursday that the Reds had
forced the Marines to yield the
western front outpost in the
Bunker Hill area guarding the
invasion route to Seoul. Vegas
is Is miles southwest of Old
Baldy, seized earlier by the Reds
in a spring drive they opened
Monday.


Associated Press Correspond
ent Forrest Edwards said shortly
after midnight it was not clear
that the Chinese were on the
crest of Vegas. The Marines
pulled back to the lower slopes
after the Chinese struck.


Some Chinese got between
Vegas and the main Marine line
but they were killed except for a
few stragglerS.


Heavy fire from both sides
echoed through the nearby low
valleys.


Friday the Marines had been
on and of Vegas in savage hand
grenade fights before smashing
to the top early Saturday after
noon. Then the Chinese struck
back just after dark Saturday.


Vegas fell Thursday night
under a Red attack that began
Monday night when $500 Chi
nese swarmed around Old Baldy,
26 miles northeast.


The Reds still hold Badly, a
red dirt target for Allied artillery
and bombs.


AS ground fighting roared on
American Sabre jets clashed with
Red MICS over North Korea,
knocking down one and damag-
ing four others, the Air Force
said.


Other American warplaneS
swept over Vegas sending rockets
and bombs tearing into the Chi
nese. Marine tanks and big guns
fired steadily.

SAIGON, Indo China. Jan.
21.-Viet Mimi guerrillas today
captured the strategic mountain
pass outpost of Dec Mong. about
275 miles north of Saigon, rout-
ing the French-led Wet Nam
garrison after an all-night
battle.


French reports said the flee
ing Wet Nam garrison in North
ern Amman suffered heavy
losses.


The dawn capture by the
Communist backed guerrillas
posed a serious threat to the
important Ankle fortress which
straddles a main supply road
halfway between Saigon and
the northern port of Haiphong.


The French have been digging
in with reinforcements around
Ankle. where they expect an all
out battle with the Red-led in
surgents. The fall of Deo Mong
gives the guerrillas an open
route over the mountains,
through which they can bring in
supplies and reinforcements
from bases in AMMAN.

PUSAN. Korea, Saturday, Jan.
S1.-A wind-fanned fire last
night ravaged the center of this
war-swollen provisional capital
of South Korea.


The fire continued past mid
night, but f1remen said early
this morning they had it under
control.


An estimated 500 shops and
frame houses were leveled.
Thousands were left homeless.
Refugees fled the area with their
meager belongings.


A United States Army officer
said there were no American cas-
ualties, but "a lot" of casualties
among Korean residents.


The fire burned out one square
mile of this port city on southern
tip of Korea. It's cause was not
Immediately determined.


Firefighters prevented the blaze
from spreading to the United
States Embassy, the main Ameri-
can servicemen's theater and the
telephone building. All are in
the vicinity.


All Pusan was plunged into
darkness when street lights failed
during the conflagration.

Only six persons have asked
clemency for the kidnap mur-
derers of Bobby Greenlease, the
Justice Department disclosed to-
day.


Officials said they have re-
ceived five letters and one tele-
gram seeking mercy in the case.
Four of the communications
asked that the death sentences
on Bonnie Brown Heady and
Carl Austin Hall be commuted;
one asked communication of the
Heady woman's sentence: and
one asked only that executions,
scheduled for next Friday in
Missouri's gas chamber, be post
poned until after Christmas.


Justice Department officials
said the couple appear to be just
about the loneliest killers in
years. An ordinary murder case,
they said, usually attracts far
more appeals for sympathy than
has the sensational Greenlease
case,

life quickly If they funk out.

active duty upor their written
request.


Non-veterans who fail fight
school get credit for the time
already served and then are re-
leased after a total Of two years.
instead of having to serve four.

PARIS. Aug. 13.-Western
Europe may have it's political
and economic troubles, it's falter-
ing governments, inflated money,
Communist pressures and uncer-
tainties about the future-but it
should have plenty to eat in the
coming year.


From Scandinavia to the
Mediterranean and from the
Atlantic to the Iron Curtain,
nearly every country reports
bumper grain crops for 1853.


Not even disastrous floods in
the Netherlands and an abnor-
mally rainy summer in Britain
and Switzerland have gravely
affected the land this year. In
the north. cold spring damaged
some crops, but the losses were
made up in a summer of good
growing weather.


Over the whole half continent,
official crop forecasts are almost
unanimously reporting better
than average" most find 1858
the best agricultural year since
the war and even better than
most prewar years.





There will be declines in some
productS-German wines, Swiss
wheat, Dutch meats and dairy
products. Austrian sugarbeets
and Italian potatoes-hut these
are balanced by gains in other
crops.

Montgomery County, Md.

Lack OF rain and the above

In addition. springs and wells

In pastures that normally

tinued since midsummer. has
most seriously affected livestock
farmers who are feeding winter
rations. and the few orchardists
in the country whose apple
crops were damaged.

dry weather. Apples, the service
reported. have been damaged
within the last three weeks. Corn,
which was we'll toward maturity

drought became apparent. is
about normal, the service said.

est hit by the drought. He said

tremely low.


"At this season." Mr.. Ander-
son said, I'VE normally expect
some stream recovery because
the forest trees are becoming
dormant. thus allowing more
water to percolate into the wells
and streams. But there hasn't
been the expected recovery"


Not All Hard Hit.


Least affected by the drought
is the section extending from
Rockville, through Brookville
and Olney. This area, Mr.. An
derson said, had several rains
during the late summer.


Joe Hutton, who farms near

fair condition.


Believe it or not" Mr.. Hutton
said, "but I have bluegrass that
is green. OF course. my fields
haven't been overgrazed.


II would say our section has
Jared better than the rest of the
county,"


James King, OF near Dawson

A narrow hailstorm, that was just
about as wide as his farm, dam
aged early hay and the drought
injured his late crops.


Like most dairymen. Mr.. King
is on winter feed and may run
short before next spring.

1881.

Perhaps the least controversial of all Dis
trict reorganization plans is that for the Metro
politan Police Department. Police Chief Murray
is not apt to criticize it for the good reason
that most of the reforms provided in the plan
already were under consideration by the chief
and his assistants. The Encouragement of units
and the creation of several new ones are de-
signed to improve the administrative efficiency
of the department, and thereby to improve the
quality of law enforcement rendered the city.


There are now II units clustered under the
direct supervision of the executive officer,
Deputy Chief Covell. Each unit is supposed to
receive the constant personal attention of the
deputy chief, but from a practical standpoint
it is physically impossible for one man to
watch closely all the varied functions involved.
They range from personnel management sup
plies and training, to the Women's Bureau, the
police radio station and civil defense activities
The II units would be consolidated into four
main divisions, the heads of each reporting to
Deputy Chief Covell. This plan would afford
the deputy chief more time for the handling
of pressing personnel and other administrative
problems for which Chief Murray holds his
deputy responsible.


Another important change would increase
from three to five the number of inspection
districts in the field. The reorganizing staff
points out that the work of the precincts has
increased tremendously since the present three
district setup was adopted, with the result that
an inspector cannot give adequate attention to
all the precincts under his general supervision
Closer scrutiny of precinct operations should
help to keep precinct commanders on their toes


The proposed administrative shakeup would
bring the department into line with model police
organizations elsewhere. Washington should
be leading, not tagging, in the field of police
administration.
headline: Police Reorganization

Search parties brought in 81

The crash of the speedy plane

the first on a scheduled CONNER

SWEA CITY. Iowa, Sept. 19.-
Fire which broke out in the Bap-

was conducting a revival meet

4, and his 18-month-old sister
Irene last night.


The father, the Rev. Everett
Beal, was seriously burned when
he rushed up a flaming stairway
in an effort to rescue the chill
dren.


Mr.. Beal and his wife were at
the Swea City Baptist Church
revival meeting just across the
street from the parsonage when
the fire was discovered.


The fire apparently started
under the stairwell. but its cause
has not been determined, Fire
Chief Lynn Pulver said.

The world will little note, but
Congress at last has remem-
bered to abolish a commission
created 18 years ago to plan a
highway connecting the Lincoln
Memorial with the Gettysburg
battlefield.


The original resolution pro-
vided that the 13-member COM
mission would expire within a
year after completion of the
parkway. The parkway never was
completed. In fact, it never was
begun. The commission merely
spent some time and $4,000
studying routes suggested by the
old Bureau of Public Roads.


The House agreed yesterday
that such deliberations would be
superfluous now in view Of State
highway improvements between
here and Gettysburg. So the
House let the old commission
perish,

three Miami horse race tracks
has been passed by the Florida
House. 1924, and sent to Gov.
Dan McCarty for signature


The bill would let Hialeah keep
the midwinter dates next year
by virtue of the first choice under
present law.


In the 1954-55 season Hialeah
would take third-choice opening
,datess now held by Tropical Park
and Gulfstream would move into
the rich middle dates. with Trop-
ical closing the season. Tropical
Park would get the middle dates
in 1955-1956.


The rotation plan was devised
in the Senate this year after
defeat there Of another bill that
would have given Gulfstream
Park a portion of the choice
dates usually allotted to Hialeah.


The fight over racing dates
has been a biennial affair in
the Florida Legislature ever
since l947, when Hialeah Park
put through bill taking assign
ment of dates out of the hands
of the State Racing Commits
sion. That law divides the
season into three 40-day periods.
with the track producing the
most revenue getting the choice
! dates.

Various reasons have been advanced from
time to time for not building Potomac River
bridge in the central area, between the Memo
rial and Key Bridges. There is only one per-
suasive reason for putting an additional span
there, namely, the demands of traffic. The
special origin and destination survey conducted
today by the District Highway Department
should settle the question as to traffic demands
The check caused showdown that was incon-
venient to motorists but, in the long run, they
should benefit.


The National Capital Planning Commis-
sion would prefer to have two fringe" bridges,
one at Alexandria and another above Key
Bridge. The theory is that these crossings
would enable through traffic to bypass down.
town Washington and that this would greatly
relieve the bottlenecks at the Fourteenth street.
Memorial and Key Bridges. The commission
also opposes any structure across Theodore
Roosevelt Island. The proposed street bridge
would cross one end of the wildlife sanctuary


The questionnaires that were distributed to
incoming motorists from Virginia will reveal
just how many through cars are using the
present bridges and whether their diversion to
some other crossing would solve the present
bridge congestion during rush hours The data
will bring up to date trafhc-load figures previ-
ously compiled by the Regional Highway Plan
ming Committee. These figures indicated the
need for another bridge to serve the downtown
section of Washington and the nearby residen-
tial areas Of Virginia. If the new study confirms

calling for another central-area crossing will
be hard to resist,

"The fifth house he painstakingly
covered with strips of bark to lure the
downy woodpecker. and put it up last.
Shortly afterwards, two little birds
spent the day carrying straw and grass
into the special downy house.


"They weren't downies. but English
sparrows, and my husband at first was
annoyed.


"The next day he went out with
thermos bottle cork, and put it in the
aperture and then opened the hinged
roof to peer into the house.


when he saw the neat, completed
little nest and the two sparrows watch
ing him from a nearby tree, he didn't
say a word but took the cork out and
tossed it off into the long grass.


THAT was month ago, and the
English sparrows. the only pair on our
farm, are very much at home. enjoy
ing their rustic downy woodpecker
house and sharing the seeds with the
other birds at the feeding stations"





Fortunately for the English SparrowS
in America, such spleen as quoted
above seldom exists any more, except
here and there.


It is realized that our native birds
are not such dullards. after all, and
that if they do not nest one place.
they nest another.


We are all, men, animals. birds, one
great family, taking many if not all
of our characteristics from the soil we
live on, the air we breathe. the water
we drink.


We are all together in the great
boat called America, and we must live
together, work together die together.
All the foreign birds are Americans,

The National Collegiate Athletic Association
has taken a sensible step backward in killing
the ee-subStitution rule for college football.
The fact that three days of thorough discussion
by the rules committee, with various other quail
ified advisers participating, brought unani-
nous vote on the action adds weight to the
judgment.


For the players themselves, and their de-
voted spectators football in the past decade
has been too intricate for pleasure. The spec
tace of platoons of specialists romping across
the field whenever the ball changed hands, or
for kickoffs and punts, has become more like a
chess game of mechanical men than test of
the athletic energy and ingenuity of band
of young Americans. The boy who spent few
minutes each Saturday afternoon holding the
ball for field goal and extra point kicks must
have been almost as frustrated as his parents
in the stands.


There have been other effects, perhaps even
more serious, the curricula of college sports
and the schools themselves. Platoon football,
as it developed under the free-subStitution rule,
required not only big squads of specialized play
ers-so specialized by physique or training that
many of them could fill only one type OF assign
ment-but also enlarged squads of coaches
equally specialized. Many schools have neither
the manpower nor the finances to support such
an athletic standing army. Some gave up
football entirely, others terminated traditional
rivalrieS.


The change now voted varies only slightly
from the substitution rule in effect prior to
1941 Players taken out in one quarter are not
eligible to return until the following quarter
except for special status given the final four
nainuAs of the second and fourth quarters

The Alexandria Fire Preven-
tion Bureau is investigating the
cause of blaze which yesterday
routed three families from the
home they shared at I'll Oro-
noco street.


Eleven persons, including two
mothers and their six small
children trapped on the Sec
ond floor of the burning
building barely escaped with
their lives. The mothers tossed
the children through second
floor windows into the waiting
arms of friends on the ground
below, then dropped through
after them.


Four of the victims were
treated at Alexandria Hospital
for burns and cuts. All three
families lost most of their pos
sessions, and were left homeless
until the house can be repaired.
Home service of the Alexandria
Red Cross Chapter stepped in
to provide some Of the victims
with clothes and temporary shell
ter.


Flames Burst Through Wall.


The fire started in the first
floor apartment occupied by Mr..
and Mrs. Edward j. Reed and
their four children, Judy Ann, 6;
Terry, 2; Dale, 8, and Bobby, 8
months. Mr.. Reed was at work
and Mrs. Reed was in the house
with the children.


Mrs. Reed told firemen Dale
was in the kitchen alone when
he saw flames burst through the
wall over the hot-water heater.
Mrs Reed saw the flames about
the same time and hustled her
four children out of the burning
building.


Trapped upstairs in one apart
ment were Mrs. Fred Perkey, her
four children, Judy. s; Wayne,
4; Treva, 2, and Elvira, 8 weeks;
her brother Frank Hilliard, 18,
his friend. Leroy Silliman, II,
and Mrs. Ruby Milliken, a guest
In the other upstairs apartment
were Mrs. Ward Taylor and her
two children, Hilda, 4, and
Linda, 2. Both Mr.. Perkey and
MI. Taylor were at work.


Flames Block Stairway.


"The first I knew of the fire
was when Ruby opened the door
to go out, and we saw flames
coming up the stairs. We couldn't
get by" said Mrs. Perkey.


Frank and Leroy broke out a
side window and dropped nearly
90 feet to the driveway below.
Several neighbors had gathered
beneath the window by then.


II threw the children out the
window to them, then jumped
out myself" said Mrs. Perkey.


Mrs. Taylor said she was un-
aware Of the fire until she looked
out the window and saw flames
against the side wall. She threw
her two small children into the
waiting arms of the crowd, then
leaped out after them. She was
cut on the leg as she hit the
ground.


Reeds Lose Everything.


Mrs. Milliken could not recall
how she got out. She was burned
on the face and hand.


Everyone was out of the build
, ing when f1remen arrived. They
brought the flames under control,
and confined them to the down.
stairs apartment and the stair
case. The upstairs was badly
damaged by smoke, however, and
most of the Perkey and Taylor
family possessions were scorched
beyond use. The Reeds lost
everything. None of the families
had insurance on their posses
sions. The house, a two-story
brick building, was leased by
Mr.. Reed from c. j. Orrison.
Mr.. Reed said he subleased the
upstairs quarters to the Perkey
and Taylor families.

officers.

The boys are from we'll to-do

One boy listened to his radio

Sometime after midnight he
slipped out of the house and went

about 10 blocks away. Using a
key hidden near the back door
to enter the house, he then woke
his partner.


Sought Unlocked Doors.


The two boys would prowl sys-
tematically through a row of
houses looking for unlocked
doors. When they entered a
home, one boy usually stood
guard while the other crept into
bedroom.


Wearing tennis shoes and car
rying small flashlights, they
looked for cash on bedroom
dressers, in closets and on night
stands.


They're lucky they weren't
shot proWling through houses
like that" Sergt. Leahy said.

SEOUL, Mar. 25.-Fighting in
a rain of American fire, Chinese
Reds broke up a two-pointed at
tack today in the bloody
trenches of Old Baldy.


At nightfall the Americans
were back where they started,
about 125 yards down the bare,
windswept western front hill.


The fighting, now in it's third
day, was vicious and deadly.


One officer said the Americans
drew Red fire every time they
popped their heads up"


AS darkness fell, infantry
fighting eased off while the big
guns of both sides slugged it out.


The Reds swept over Old
Baldy Monday night and the
Americans have been trying to
get it back since.


Attack Stopped Cold.


One American attack force
pushed off this morning toward
a Red trench network on the
northeast and was stopped cold.


Another lashed out toward the
northwest. A division officer
said this one "got close" but was
finally ordered back in the after
noon when the going got too
rough"


It was trench-fighting, blaze
of close-quarter grenade and
small arms fire.


The officer said there are ap-
parently two Red companies on
Baldy holding two trench net
works. The Americans hold the
other.


Associated Press Correspond
ent Stan Carter reported from
the 7th Division that American
tanks pushed around the flank
of the hill to cut up Chinese
reinforcements.


The Reds were reported TAX
ing heavy casualties but so were
American and Colombian units
of the 7th Division.


A stream of wounded moved to
the rear. Helicopters shuttled
from the front to hospitals and
back again.


The United States 9th Army
said Red bunkerS on the hill
were taking a savage pounding.


B-26 light bombers started
radar-directed strikes this morn
ing, one every 20 minutes.


The Chinese made their move
Monday night along a 6-mile
strip against the hill mass west
OF Chorwon that guards the in
vasion route to Seoul.


On Pork Chop. T-Bone and
other hills the $500 Reds were
beaten back in the darkness.


Then the battle came to head
at Old Baldy.


U. N. Troops Fall Back.


American and Colombian
troops, fighting heroically, fell
back from the top early Tuesday
under waves of Chinese.


Reinforcements rushed to the
battlefield.


The artillery fire was the
heaviest since the terrible battle
for the Kumhwa ridges five
months ago.


Allied officers had no estimates
for Red casualties on Baldy, but
said they believed the other
fighting Monday and Tuesday
cost the Reds at least one-third
and possibly more of their $500
man force.

CHICAGO. Aug. "A small
airplane, which police said was
stolen, crashed in a north side
residential district yesterday.
critically injuring the pilot.


The plane plunged to a street
two blocks from the pilots home
and near the Chicago Cubs
Wrigley Field.


Police said the pilot, Edmund
w, Cross, %. flew low over the
area for Is minutes before the
two-Seater light plane fell
through trees and power lines to
the street.


The plane had been stolen
earlier from Sky Haven airport,
northwest of Chicago. police said.
No charge has been placed
against Cross.


Police said Cross told attend
ants at the airport he had per-
mission of the planes owner,
Richard Lloyd. to use the craft.
The owner said he had not given
him permission.


The authorities said Cross
took the plane up after a round
of taverns with a companion,
who was found sleeping in
Cross car at the airport.


Before the crash, residents of
the North Side section were ter
rified as the plane skinned over
rooftops, trees and utility lines.

tered on Frances demand that

uniform, 2-million-man West

overseas possessions are threat

4 MI. Adenauer fears this would

session with Mr.. Adenauer.

! spokesman last night said that

army treaty "have been very
much exaggerated" He in
dicated they did not revise or
alter basically the pact, which

Prague radio announced a

first secretary of the party's
Central Committee and thus re-
tanned control of the powerful
party organization.

government since Zapotocky

ent Gottwald last March and

mergers was that of the two
security portfolios-interior and
national Security-into a single
powerful interior ministry

VERSAILLES, France, Dec.
, 1.-THE first round of balloting
by the French Parliament today
failed to select a president for
the nation.


The first ballot was seen as
merely a test of strength and a
basis for bargaining in SUBJ
sequent rounds.


Eight candidates were an
nounced to succeed Socialist
Vincent Auriol in the seven-year
post of great prestige but few
real powers. There was a pos
sibility that several others might
enter the field, and also that a
voting deadlock might produce
other compromise choices.


BalIOting Process Slow.


Under Frances multi-party
system, none of the nine factions
holds anything like a majority
of the 946 seats in the National
Assembly and the Council of
the Republic (Senate). Since
each member must walk to the
rostrum singly to cast his vote,
each ballot takes about four
hours. Two a day is about the
maximum.


Parliament met in the As
sembly Hall, built in 1871 in the
open courtyard of the palace,
10 miles from Paris. Voting is
secret, the winner the first man
to get a majority of the votes
cast. There are no campaign
speeches.


Heretofore no more than two
ballots have been needed since
France started electing preSi-
dents under the Third Republic.
The second vote has been neces-
sary only four times.


This time, veteran observers
expected no decision before the
third, or possibly the fourth, vote.


8 Official Candidates.


These were the announced
official candidates:


Premier Joseph Laniel, right
of center independent; Foreign
Minister Georges Bidault, backed
by his Catholic Popular Repub-
lican Movement (MRP); Social
ist Marcel Naegelen. former Gov
ernor General of Algeria; Jean
Medecin, Radical Socialist Mayor
of Nice; Independent Jacques

Union; Yvon Delbos, former

Party: Marcel Cachin, 84-year-
old Communist and the oldest

bly,, and Senator Jean Kalb, put
forward today by the Gaullist
Union for the Republican Social
Action (URAS).


Another Radical Socialist cam
didate, Fine Arts Minister Andre
Cornu, withdrew last night.

The troubles followed a gov

rency and issuing new money

Every Czech was obliged to ex-

to so crowns for one new one,

savings.

sources, said workers at the giant
Skoda armaments plant began
demonstrating June 1.-The Mon

rency announcement.


Raising the Stars and Stripes,
the reports said, the workers
stormed the town hall, tore down
pictures of Communist heroes
and burned the city's archives.
They also repeatedly destroyed
large amounts of machinery in
the armament plant.


The rioting lasted until June S
and was ended only when extra
police and troops set up machine
guns throughout the city.

cake are coming in-not enough,

stockmen around Big Spring
have received drought emergency

how many cattle and sheep the
stockman has and how much
feed he needs.


Texas has 152 counties
almost two-thirds of its 263, ,644

Eisenhower designated them as

A OF them have had pretty good

But-"general rains are still
needed before the extreme
drought is relieved" said Louis
P. Merrill, Fort Worth, regional
director Of the Soil Conservation
Service.


At Lubbock, 100 miles south

agreed the feed program was
successful.

ut looks like the little feed

w. Floyd Deacon said the

not only Tor colored Americans.

TOKYO, Sunday, Jan. 25.-
Russian and United States air
men are glaring at each other
through gunSights across one
minute of space.


One incident after another
has brought tension to the
swapping point in the air from
tiers high over Northern Japan,
the islands Russia occupies close
to Japan and Communist China.
It would seem that efforts to
conf1ne the air war to Korea
are failing, bit by bit. Fighting
in the skies could break out
anywhere in the Far East where
Communist and United Nations
air patrols meet.


In the recent past, Russian
fighter plane shot down one
United States Superfort in the
waters off northern Japan. The
fighter came from the Kuriles
or Sakhalin, both but a minutes
flying time away.


Planes Shot Down.


Last week a Navy Neptune pa
troll bomber was brought down
by Chinese Communist shore
batteries in Formosa Strait.


The Communists announced
on the heels of this incident that
they had shot down B-29 Su-
perfort out of the skies over
Manchuria. The United States
Air Force said its bomber was
over Korea.


Japan and the United States
have warned Russia that any of
her planes caught inside Japa-
nese territory would be shot
down.


Peiping, rejecting Russian pol
icy, long has shown a great deal
of interest and nervousness
about Japanese rearmament and
American defense efforts in the
imperial islands, particularly the
northernmost island of Hokkaido.


One Peiping broadcast styled
Japan's stern warning on un-
authorized flights over the coun-
try "crudely camouf1aged war
provocation designed in the
U. S. A."


SkirmisheS at Hand.


What is the significance be-
hind these events?


Has the preliminary sparring
actually begun for World War
III?


A look at the record shows
the best Communist planes out
here are RuSSian-made and GER
tainly Russiano-flown when they
fly from Soviet bases. The best
United Nations planes are United
States made and piloted.


Thus a sort Of bootleg air skir-
mish between Russian and Amer
lean pilots already has begun just
north of Japan.


The fact that Russia has bases
on Sakhalin Island, one minute
by jet from northern Japan,
where United States Air Force
planes are based, means an in
ternational incident could occur
at almost any moment.
Both Russian and American
Air Forces obviously have orders
to shoot, provided the other side
invades their territory.


This sparring could very well
be the jabbing which usually
takes place before the main bout

PARIS, June 19.-President
Vincent Auriol sharply told
Frances political leaders today
to put aside their jealousies and
pickering and map out an agreed
program which will bring an end
to the country's 30-day cabinet
crisis.


The President acted after the
National Assembly had thrown
out his fourth candidate for the
job-Radical Socialist Andre
Marie-early this morning. Mr..
Marie got only 272 votes, far
short of the 314 needed for in
vestiture. Paul Reynaud, Pierre
Mendes-France and Georges
Bidault had been defeated before
him.


The President, largely a fig
urehead who usually acts only as
a moderator, called in 20 of the
most influential deputies in the
National Assembly and bluntly
told them they must work out a
solution among themselves.


He said continuation of the
crisis is running the risk of
. damaging the Republic and
weakening France both in the
French union and the world"


Communists Excluded.


In the group he assembled
were all the Premiers since the
war, men who have been nomi-
mated for the job but turned
down by the National Assembly,
and heads of the political parties.
Only the Communists were ex-
cluded.


After the verbal dressing down,
President Auriol directed the II
former Premiers and defeated
candidates to sit down around
a table and draw up a program,
in cooperation with the parties.
When the program is completed,
the President said he would then
name the man to put it in
effect.


In the group ordered to ham,
mer out the policy outline were:
Rene Mayer, Andre Marie,
Georges Bidault, Rene Pleven,
Antoine Pinay, Henri Queuille,
Pierre Mendes-France, Paul Rey-
maud, Jules Moch, Edgar Faure

ator Carlson said.


Among the proposals was one

employees.


Somewhat along the line of
the original Hoover Commission
proposals on pay, the recommen-
dation would set up a compen-
sation board within the Civil
Service Commission. Less atten-
ton would be paid elaborate job
descriptions as provided in the
present Classification Act.


Instead, pay would be based
on the type of job and the pay
Of comparable jobs in the local
ity where a Federal worker was
employed. Another factor would
be the jobs Importance in the
labor market where the employe
worked.


Congress would set the mini
mum and maximum Federal pay
rates, but the compensation
board would set rates for all in
dividual employees within the
floor and ceiling and could adj
just the salaries from time to
time.

nameplate was heightened to

decades than anyone can re-

Times was nudging over toward
sensationalism.


The Manchester Guardian, an

to news on page one and ads in
side last September, upsetting a
131-year custom.

trenches.


Swift American f1ghter-bom-

How much Washington contributed to the
career of Marjorie Kinnan Rawlings may be
matter of debate, but she never wholly lost her
interest in the city in which she was born and
in which she received her earliest training as a
writer. Many years after she left the District
she told local friend that The Star was the
first newspaper she could remember. She read
it's Sunday supplement in the days when it's
contributors included Rudyard Kpling, Arthur
Conan Doyle, H. G. Wells and jacques Futrelle
of "The Thinking Machine" Whether she
gained her inspiration for the art of fiction
from that group of masters is q question, but
nobody doubts that her purpose was developed
while she still was girl.


She went to the University of Wisconsin to
learn the tricks of the authors trade. After
graduation in 1918, she did publicity work for
the YMCA, hammered out articles for United
Features and several other SyndicateS and was
for a while a sob sister" reporter. 1t was
not until 1923 that she discovered the secret of
producing copy which magazines of national
circulation would buy. The Florida background
which she adopted as her own gave her line"
which she exploited with notable success South
Moon Under" appeared in 1888, Golden Apples"
in 1885 BY this latter date she had achieved
technical maturity. "The Yearling," issued in
1888 brought her the Pulitzer prize and the
first "'big money" she ever had earned


And these rewards certainly were deserved.
Writing never was easy for Mrs. Rawlings. Her
picture of Jody Baxter, his pet fawn Flag, his
desperate and pitiful parents and their neigh
bors, human and animal, was the fruit of self
evident agony. She confessed that she 'sweated
blood" over it. The same observation probably
applies to her last efforts If they failed to win
popular acclaim, it was not because they were
deficient in authentic values.


Now Mrs Rawlings passes into the history
of her country and her era. She leaves at least
one supremely fine accomplishments grand
performance which not soon will fade.
headline: Marjorie Rawlings

SEOUL, June 26.-At least 49,
900 Chinese Reds hit Allied lines
on both ends Of the Korean bat
tlefront today, but hard-fighting
South Koreans hurled back most
Of 10000 Communists who at
tackled eight strategic outposts
in the west.


United States Saber jets shot
down two Communist MIG jets
and damaged one in air battles
over North Korea this afternoon.


The big-scale Red assaults
opened the fourth year of war on
this battered peninsula.


Heavy fighting still ragged on
the east-central front, where
5000 Communists attacked ROK
positions near the junction of the
Pukhan and Kumsong Rivers.


Attacks, Aimed at ROK.


It was in this sector that 80, 900

years.

attacks left United States and
other foreign troops virtually
untouched and concentrated on

assault fell on allied lines block
ing one of the old invasion

said most of the Chinese were
thrown back from eight i'm
portant hill outposts west of
Yonchon, in the Little Nori and
Old Baldy sector.


Incomplete reports from the
front said the Reds had lost
3,700 men killed and wounded
up to 7 am.


The South Koreans lost some
ground during the night, but re-
grouped and counterattacked,
driving the Reds down the hills,
the Army said.


Fighting RACES on Hills.

Chinese knocked South Koreans
off three front-line positions
near the Pukhan -Kumsong River
junction. Counterattacking South
Koreans twice drove to the crest

VIENNA. Austria, Feb. 21.-
Thirty top Jewish Communists
in Hungary were reported to-
night either to have committed
suicide or otherwise fallen victim
to a purge dictated by a visiting
Russian group.


The advices came from diplo-
matte and usually reliable un-
official sources, who presented
them as not fully confirmed but
the best available information
from the neighboring Communist
nation.


The same sources reported a
growing economic crisis in Hun
gary. long lines of persons before
bread stores and the threat of
real hunger late in the spring.
BY their accounts:


The 80 Jewish Communists
were removed one way or another
from their high posts by a group
of Russian burgers who arrived
in Budapest several weeks ago.
They were rumored sent because
fully 80 per cent of the top Off
cialS Of the Hungarian Com
muniSt regime are jews. includ-
ing Premier Matyas Rakosi.


Some Victims Executed.


The 80 allegedly were "sus-
pected zionists' and, throughout
the east European Soviet bloc,
Communism has been attacking
Jews suspected of the slightest
sympathy for Israel.


Some of the group killed them
selves. others disappeared. some
were arrested and some were ex-
ecuted by firing squads.


Reported suicides: Zoltan Vas,
head of the state economic plan
ming office. and 10 high officers
of the political police.


Reported executions: 1t. Gen.
Peter Gabor, head Of the secret
police. said to have been shot
together with his wife and chill
dren. His wife was a private
secretary in Premier Rakosi's
Office.


Reported arrests: Gen. Sander
Nogradi, deputy defense minis
ter; and six high officers of the
state security Office including
Col. zoltan Megyeri.


Others Reported Arrested.


Also reported arrested: Ist-
van Szirmai, chief of the Hun
garian state radio and four de-
partment chiefs; DR.. Benedek,
chief of the Jewish hospital in
Budapest; DR.. Istvan Balint,
chief physician Of a political po-
lice hospital in Budapest; eye
specialist Istvan Loewi.


Reported missing from their
offices: Karoly Kiss, former
foreign minister, and Arpad
Hazi, former interior minister.
Both were denoted last year to
vice premiers.


Recently dismissed: Justice
Minister Gyula Decsi.


Reported fallen from grace:
Foreign Minister Eric Molnar
who, however, was in his Office
earlier this week.


According to the reports, Zol-
tan Vas committed suicide after
he was ousted earlier this week
from the planning Office. His
Office is partly responsible for
the economic crisis which diplo-
matte sources say has created
dissatisfaction and brought on
MoscoW's wrath.

VICKSBURG, Miss, Dec. S.
Flashlights probed nervously
along tornado-tortured stretch
of the main street here tonight,
prying into ripped buildings for
dead and injured.


Sodden Christmas decorations
and toys Uttered the dark streets
and sidewalks. Bricks were tum-
bled everywhere. Some of the
debris still pressed on the
crushed tops of parked cars.


In City Hall, anxious relatives
milled in silent anguish, waiting
for official word of a missing
loved one. Many others roamed
the streets.


The four Observation-Disclosures,
Lutheran, Mercy, Charity-oper-
ated under emergency lights. The
power system went out with the
sudden storm, natures most fe-
rocious.


Some Power Restored.


Late tonight, power had been
restored in much of the city but
not in the section at least four
blocks long right in the center of
this city of 27,9OO persons.


Christmas shoppers, their
numbers somewhat reduced by
late afternoon rain, were in the
stores when the tornado hit.


1t came without warning. In
an instant the peaceful scene
was bedlam. Women screamed;
clerks and customers scrambled
for the exits.


The twister rumbled northeast
across the Mississippi River,
grinding first into Mulberry
street nearest the river and
parallel to it.


Then it moved on into Wash



ington street. a main business
section parallel to Mulberry and
the next block over. Three other
blocks were heavily damaged.


Guardsmen Aid.


National Guardsmen, sent in
to help in rescue work and pa
troll the stricken area, probed the
ruins. along with an army of
volunteers.


The scene. hours after the
twister struck, was still chaotic.
Officials feared the rescue
crews would turn up more bodies
when the dawn rolled in.

ernment for development of still

market-and out of the way Of

The time to apply strawberry
pest control measures is early,
experts say, when the fruit buds
begin to form in the spring and
before the fruit forms.


Killing the pests early, they
say, will eliminate the need for
applying poisonous sprays when
the fruit is forming, and reduce
or eliminate the possibility of
causing off-flavor in the fruit.


It's Just at this time, when
the buds are forming, that the
millipedes, plant bugs, Spittle-
bugs and weevils cause the most
serious damage.


Yields Increase.


The advantages of proper
spraying are obvious, the experts
point out, since spraying for in
Sects and disease in Kentucky
and North Carolina has in
creased yields by 80 to 81 crates
an acre.


A more important reason for
applying control measures early
is that insecticides cannot be
applied to ripening fruit with
safety to the consumer"


Chlordane, DDT and toxa-
phene have proved effective
against the pests and will not
affect the fruit if applied early,
the experts say.


Spring Is the Time.


The time to apply the meas
ures is when the temperature is
above IS degrees and the insects
are active, about the time people
have "sprlng fever" the straw
berry specialists advise.


Spittlebugs and millipedes are
not too active until the fruit
forms. but they can be killed
while they are small and before
the fruit is present.

The Reds threw elements of

can skies without finding a Com

TIME HAS a habit Of slipping away
i all too quickly. It doesn't seem like
II years have passed since our ship, a
small, overcrowded transport, docked
at Honolulu.


The city. with its gayly colored build
ings and bright roofs, seemed to rise
from the sea as the convoy approached.
Tall palms waved in the warm breeze.
The various Towering trees were in
bloom amid waxy-green foliage.


Behind the city, white, fieecy clouds,
with bright blue sky for their back
ground, clung to the rugged mountain
tops.


To be sure, the wounds of the Pearl
Harbor attack still were fresh and the
islands were girding for war. But, even
so, it was just as books and travel fold
ers pictured it-Diamond Head, Wal
kaiki Beach, the welcoming hula girls,
exotic foods.


Honolulu looked mighty good that
bright Sunday morning, particularly
after the convoy's mild tussle with a
submarine the day before.

LONDON, Feb. IA. - Britain
has promised France she will
look into proposals aimed at en-
suring as close as possible Brit
ish cooperation with the six
nation European army project.


A communique issued last
night at the end Of top-level
British French talks, said
French suggestions for tighten
ing British bonds with the Eur
opean Defense Community will
be explored in diplomatic ses-
sions Ito take place shortly"


France also asked Britain for
money and material aid in her
war against the Wet Mimi reh-
els in Indo China but the Lon
don government gave no immed-
late answer on this plea.


Premier Rene Mayer, Foreign
Minister Georges Bidault and
Economics Minister Robert Bu-
ron represented France at the
talks here. Foreign Secretary
Anthony Eden led the British
side, supported by Defense Min
lister Lord Alexander and Board
of Trade President Peter Thor
neycroft.


Britain is not a member of the
EDO, which includes France,
Germany. Italy, Belgium, the
Netherlands and Luxembourg.
The London government has ex-
pressed support for the project
but has SHE'D away from full
membership because of her ma
jor commitments in other parts
of the world.


Many members of the French
parliament, fearing the possi-
bility that France may some day
have to face a rearmed Germany
alone. have expressed concern
that Britain has not Signed the
EDO pact. which calls for the
inclusion of 100000 German
troops in the European army.


France and Germany have
both signed the treaty but
neither has yet ratified it.
