GREAT FALLS, Mont, June
4.-Raging mountain streams
drove residents of three villages
to the hills and threatened to
inundate a greater area Of West
Great Falls early today.
Rains which measured 4.24
inches here the last three days
stopped falling at ESQ am,
(MST), but forecasters said
more downpours were expected
over the flood area east of the
continental divide in Northwest
Montana.


Villagers were driven from
Tracy, 6 miles southeast of
Great Falls; Niehart, SO miles
southeast. and Monarch, 13
miles farther southeast.


One man was reported to have
died of a heart attack at Tracy,
which was without telephone
communications.


Sandbagging efforts along the
Sun River were washed out last
night in West Great Falls. a
separate municipality adjoining
Great Falls. It was estimated
30 residential blocks were under
water there.

Louisiana's coastal lowlands
faced a new flood crisis from the
Gulf of Mexico today as rising
streams to the north forced
$4,000 persons from their homes
In a multi-million-dollar flood.


While swollen bayouS and rivers
poured tons of water toward the
Gulf, the coastal residents braced
against the possibility of inunda-
ton from wind-whipped tides.


Observers believed the crisis
would come today. If tides re-
main moderate another "a hours
they think there is chance that
streams and backwater areas can
handle tidewater.


The threat centers around
Crowley, in southwest Louisiana.
Overlooking bayous have forced
excavations at Merentau, Evan
geline, Midland and Esterwood
and sent the flood tapping into
the outskirts of Crowley.


High Winds Predicted.


The weather bureau predicted
winds from the South, putting
the area in extreme danger if
tides are high.


The stricken area was a broad
belt arching from the southwest
corner of the State, near the
Texas border, through central
Louisiana to the east central
boundary with Mississippi. The
belt is more than 200 miles long
and 100 miles wide at points.


Major rivers in Louisiana were
not at critical stages, but almost
a foot of rain over the week end
sent already swollen smaller
streams out of their banks and
blanketed almost a foot of water
on this States many low areas.
There was nowhere for it to go.


Then water began draining
from the hilly areas into the sub
merged lowlands-the rich cot
ton and rice producing areas.


Damage S1OO Million.


Damage to the States rich cot
ton and rice crops was estimated
at 500 million. The floods also
caused millions of dollars damage
to highways, private property
and livestock.


Storms which swept over
Southern areas over the week end
moved northeastward and show
ers and thundershowerS we're re-
ported early today along the East
Coast from Virginia northward
to Philadelphia.


Heaviest rainfalls in the last
"a hours were in Tennessee and
Virginia, with nearly two inches
in some areas. Two small tor
nadoes hit Southern sections
Tuesday. One twister f1attened
a house and three barns near
Griffin. Ga. A second tornado
struck at Pensacola. Fla. dam
aging a skating rink and resi-
dence.

In voting for an unprecedented $40 million
bond issue to finance a countrywide sewerage
system, Fairfax County has shown a deter
mination to keep step with sanitation progress
in nearby Virginia. It's present crazy quilt of
separate community systems and septic tanks,
many of the latter dangerously overloaded,
has put the county at disadvantage in this
era of expanding residential and industrial
development across the Potomac River. Only
an integrated sewerage network of the type
planned by county engineers could meet the
threat to public safety and prosperous growth
inherent in inadequate sanitation facilities.


AS was expected the rural sections of the
county were outvoted by the urbanized sections
In the latter areas the need for better sewerage
had become acute with the continued con-
struction of homes, apartments and shopping
centerS But the rural residents also will
benefit from the improvement program through
improved property values and better health
conditions. And only those who use the new
sewers will pay for them, under the self
hquidating plan for paying off the heavy loan.
The integrated sewerage program is logical
corollary of the county's recent decision to join
with Alexandria in building joint sewage
disposal facilities.
headline: Fairfax Keeps Step

ried a passenger. Five persons witnessed this
Launching of humanity into new dimension

selves realized the definitive significance OF
their achievement. Months later those bicycle
boys from Dayton" announced that they were
willing to sell "all their inventions for 100000
Nobody accepted the offer, and they finally
withdrew it.

hundred papers-and was printed by very few.

SEOUL, Sunday, July 26.-An
unusual 12-hour lull in the fight
ing on the Korean central front
was shattered by a series of Chi
nese battalion attacks against
American and South Korean
troops late Saturday night and
allied artillery roared back into
action.


Front line dispatches said
about 5000 Chinese Reds took
part in the assaults northeast of
Kumhwa, pivotal allied position
on the east central front.


The first battalion (750 mem
hit at II pm. after heavy artil-
lery fire against the United States
Sd Division about eight miles
northeast of KumhWa.


Brisk Fighting Reported.


Less than 10 minutes later
another Chinese battalion and
two more companies 1920 mem
struck against Korean defenders
several miles farther east on the
new Kumsong front, near Sam
Hyon Hill.


During the same period Ko-
rean and American troops near
Kumhwa reported brisk fights
and several contacts with Chi
nese platoons.


Massed allied artillery, which
had fallen into almost complete
silence during the evening. sud-
denly roared into action at the
first Chinese shelling and ad-
vance. The sky from Kumhwa
to Kumsong was brilliant with
flares and allied searchlights.
No Word on Progress.


There was no immediate re-
port on the progress of the Chi
nese attacks.


Shooting had dropped and ten
sion rose across parts of the front
as stronger and stronger rumors
filtered up to the line from Seoul
and Hokyo that an armistice
agreement was imminent.


But in possibly the waning
hours of the 37-month-old war,
United Nations warplanes, de-
flying blustery weather, relent-
lessly bombed Red frontline po-
sitions and supply lines.


Near the truce talk site at
Panmunjom, big guns dueled
furiously.


800 Missions Flown.


United States 5th Air Force
planes flew more than 800 mis-
Sions through the stormy
weather, dumping bomb loads
with electronic and radar sights


The Air Force said 10 allied
planes went down in Communist
territory during the week ended
yesterday. Two were Sabre jets
lost in air combat with Red fight
ers. Seven planes-three Thun-
derjets, two Pantherjets, two
Sabres-were downed by ground
fire, and one Sabre was lost to
unexplained causes, the Air
Force reported.

But here is how the maneuver

White House communiques and
reports from correspondents kept
far from the actual battle line:


Having learned last session that
a "forward-looking, progressive"
legislative program can advance
smoothly only if potential opposi-
ton is removed through careful
negotiation, the President invited
to the White House all Republican
leaders and committee chairmen.'

Servative wing.

the White House staff explained
to the Congressman what they
would like to include in the an
nual State-of-the- Union message
the outline of the Presidents
legislative program. The guests
were invited to criticize and sug-
gest.


All comment was carefully noted,
but apparently no final decisions
were sought. The final speech
would be worked out between now
and January when it is Sched-
uled for delivery. The polished
message would probably be tai
lored to congressional views, not
necessarily catering to all opinions,
but perhaps saying as much as
possible without creating unnec-
eSSary conflict.


There was one good indication
that the White House was not
seeking showdowns last week:
congressman we're not leaking
news of the conferences with their
customary freedom. If they had
had gripes to register, they would
have "told all' to the press, put
ting their own opposition views in
properly favorable light.


The Presidents statements to
the press were not particularly
revealing. He announced what
topics had been covered and prom
iSed program that will be "suc-
cessful, sound and productive. 4"
There was no hint of controversy


So the big push probably will
not begin until January Z, and
even then the White House forces
might ease gently, but gently, into
the fray. Meanwhile, it was hoped,
the opposition will have melted
away.

orphaned international Long
shoremen's Association QLA)

Hartley injunction which halted

this unions fight with the AFL

ousted from the AFL for failure

elements the AFL then chartered

week. The piers. were left idle

wharveS.

ernment added, could lead to
complete paralysis of the New
York harbor.

lila next Tuesday.

inal Today order restraining the

VATICAN CITY, Oct. 31.-
The Vatican said tonight the
Most Rev. Antonin Pawlowski
has been bishop of the Ro-
man Catholic Church for two
years, whether or not recog-
nized by the government of Com
munlst Poland.


The Warsaw Radio, as heard
last night in Vienna, said the
Polish government has appointed
him Bishop of Wroclaw (Bres-
lau).


Vatican authorities said there
apparently is some error in that
announcement. They pointed
out:


l. Only the Pope can appoint
a bishop.


2. Bishop Pawlowski was so
appointed two years ago, but
as bishop of Wloclawek, not of
Wroclaw-they are two different
cities.


3. Since the appointment, the
Polish government has pre-
vented Bishop Pawlowski from
assuming his diocese.


4. The Vatican recognizes any
Polish appointment changing
his diocese.


Authorities here believed the
announcement from Warsaw
probably was in error. or in
correctly understood. They said
it seemed more probable that
the Polish government may
finally have decided to accept
Bishop Pawlowski's papal nomi-
nation.

ROME, Dec. 12.-Striking gov

million industrial workers have
been ordered to lay down their
tools Tuesday in follow-up
show of labor strength.


Both Communist and non-Red
unions have backed the twin "a

pay.

SEOUL, Sunday, June T.
South Korean infantrymen,
battling at close quarters by the
light of flares, early today re-
gained more than half the east
ern front ground they lost to
North Korean Reds yesterday.


Frontline reports said the ROK
troops drove the Communists
back 800 yards, regrouDed. and
again pushed their counter
attack slowly forward.


The Reds drove 500 yards into
allied territory east of Luke the
Cooks Castle yesterday. The
South Koreans launched their
counteroffensive Saturday night.


Truce Buffer Zone.


Three miles to the east, about
ITS North Koreans aimed a two
pronged blow at a hill position
held by the ROKs. A United
States 9th Army briefing officer
said they retreated 10 minutes
later after losing % killed and
IL wounded.


This continuing Red punch in
the east, made while reports
from Panmunjom indicated
near agreement on an armistice.
suggested the possibility the
Communists were bidding for a
new truce buffer-zone.


In recent weeks, Chinese and
North Koreans have captured
more than a dozen allied out
posts and three mail line posi-
tions. The lost territory, how
ever, amounts to only a few
square miles.


Quarter Mile Penetration


In a smashing attack yester-
day, between 75O and 1000
North Koreans overran three
South Korean outposts ahead Of
the main line. Then the REIN
forced Red battalion socked into
the line itself in four spots east
of Luke the Cooks Castle, some
20 miles inland from the east
coast.


The Reds drove more than a
quarter mile deep into allied
territory in a two-pronged at
tack in which they hit at points
about 500 yards apart. The line
between the penetrations sagged
and the Reds poured through.


Fighting has been almost con-
tinuous in the rugged eastern
sector since Monday when the
Reds got their first foothold on
an outcropping ridge of Luke's
Castle. BY last night, the Reds
held about half of the forward
ridge.


On the eaSt-central front,
soldiers of the 5th Korean Divi-
sion fought desperately against
about 750 Chinese Reds for an
outpost on Bloody Ridge, 13
miles east of Kumsong.

pennsylvania is willing to

typhoon swept over Japan's main
island last night and early to-
day. sideswiped the teeming
Tokyo area and left in it's wake
millions of dollars in property
damage and at least lis dead,
including l American soldier.


Skies cleared today as the
storm sWirled into the North
Pacific where it began breaking
up.


The American soldier drowned
at Camp MaiZuru in Southern
Japan. His name was withheld
and details of the drowning
were not Immediately available.
japanese national police said
the big storm, with 90-mile-an-
hour winds at its center, left
ia Japanese dead, 288 missing
and 259 injured.


Hundreds of thousands of
Japanese were left homeless.


American Bases Damaged.
American bases in Japan suf-
fered damage estimated officially
at millions of dollars.


A United States Army spokes-
man said damage at Camp Otsu
near Tokyo will run to $1.9
million.


A landslide damaged the heat
ing plant and an ammunition
depot at Camp Misuru.


Five warehouses collapsed at
the Kobe quartermaster depot.
Thirty-eight United States
Army buildings in Tokyo were
damaged, six small buildings
were destroyed and three Army
Sedans were damaged.


Only minor damage was re-
ported at United States Air
Force bases. Some roofs were
lost and several Quonset huts
destroyed at Itami Air Base
near Osaka


Communications Disrupted.


Communications between
Japan and Korea were disrupted
by the storm. One Army tele-
type line was temporarily re-
paired this afternoon, but it
broke down again.


Some news copy reached
Tokyo from Korea via a British
commercial telegraph firm which
routed messages through Hong
Kong.


The Japanese coast guard said
10 small ships or boats were
sunk, but only two seamen were
known dead.


The 10,000-ton tanker Chigusa
Maru, which called for help dur
ing the height of the storm last
night, radioed today that she
had repaired a disabled engine
and was heading for port under
her own power.

scattered and small.


1t was significant that rising
prices lured in buying. Volume

Mrs. Viola Spottswood, wife OF
Bishop Stephen Gill Spottswood
of the African Episcopal Zion
Church, died in a fire early today
at her home, 1881 Sixteenth
street NV.


Mrs. Spottswood, 54. colored,
apparently had gone into the
basement apartment where the
fire was, thinking her two grand
children were there. The chill
dren, however, were safely out of
the apartment.


The fire burned out two rooms
in the basement apartment,
where the Spottswoods' daugh-
ter, Mrs. Alleyne Nixon, lived
with her children, Stephen, S,
and York, 4.


Bishop Spottswood, who lives
on the first floor, found his wife
on the bathroom floor soon after
he returned from notifying the
Fire Department. He discovered
the fire about $50 am.


Mrs. Spottswood was active in
church affairs and was district
supervisor.

A 22-year-old mother of three
children was strangled into un-
consciousness and raped in her
bed in Prince Georges County
early today.


Prince Georges police issued a
lookout for a short, stocky, COL
ored man.


The woman, who also is four
months pregnant. was asleep in
her apartment in the $500 block
of Greig street, Gregory Estates,
an apartment development in
Seat Pleasant. The man en-
tered bedroom window,
crossed the room where the
three children were sleeping,
walked across a hallway and
entered the Woman's bedroom.


Her husband had gone to work
two hours before.


Used Shirt to Choke Her.


The assailant used a shirt to
choke her. After recovering con-
SciouSneSS, her screams aroused
a neighbor, but by that time the
rapist had fled.


She was treated at Leland
Memorial Hospital for cuts,
bruises and shock.


Meanwhile, Alexandria police
today were looking for an early
morning prowler who attacks
women while they sleep. Three
such incidents have occurred in
as many months.


Awakened by Blow.


The latest attack occurred
about 3::35 am. today at 80
South Pitt street. The victim,
Mrs. Liza Paluch. 30, told police
she was awakened by blow on
the head. She said a strange
man was standing beside her bed
and struck her about 10 times
before her screams drove him
away.


Police said the man had
climbed through window of the
first floor. propping the window
open with a stick.


Two similar attacks have been
reported in the old section of
town during the past three
months. Police said they believe
the same man is responsible for
all three cases.

Frances military dilemma in
Indo- China was clear in the last
fortnight's action in North Wet
Nam.


From their insecure base in the
Tonkin Delta, the French are try
ing desperately to carry the war to
the Wet Mimi. But until native
Wet NameSe troops are trained in
such numbers as to give them a
larger numerical superiority, the
French are operating on a shoe
string.


The outside world learned early
last week that a strategic Franco
Wet Namese garrison in the heart
of the delta had been virtually
wiped out fortnight ago by a
Wet Mini regiment operating
within the French-held delta. Air
and ground reinforcements were
brought up and the Wet Mimi were
chased OF, removing the immedi-
ate threat to the important Hal
phong-Hanoi highway, railroad
and river junction.


Bod Time in. West


Meanwhile, in Western Wet
Nam, the French evacuated Lai
Chau, a symbolic tribal stronghold,
and moved to Dien Bien Phu, a
newly secured base nearby. The
new French position is claimed
to be better situated for both
offense and defense. From here
the French and Wet Namese hope
to resist any new Wet Mimi thrust
at Laos, and also to recruit tribes
men for guerrilla war against the
Reds.


The Communist rebels already
are contesting the French hold on
Dien Bien Phu. Wet Mimi columns
were attacking from the north
and south yesterday.

HANOI, Indo- China, Dec. 81.
The French today reported
their first stable clash with the
Communicated Wet Mimi at
Diem Bien Phu-the last major
French position in Northwest
1ndo-China and perhaps the first
objective of the winter rebel
campaign.


The French said patrols NOV
ing out from their heavily forti-
fled position on the plain lust
north of Laos fought for more
than an hour with rebel units
they encountered. The French
claimed 81 Wet Mimi dead and
said their own losses were light,


Foe Forced to Retreat.
= Mobile artillery and fighter
planes finally forced the Wet
Mimi to retreat. the French said.


The Wet Mimi yesterday were
reported active close to Diem
B1en Phu for the first time since
French paratroopers grabbed
the post and its airstrip five
weeks ago. Since then the
French have poured men and
arms into it.


News of the Wet Mini activ-
ity there aroused speculation
that it was the rebels first ma
Jor target and that their dash
across central Laos to the Me-
kong River last week was a
diversion to draw off French
forces.


French Air Attack Pressed.


French planes, meanwhile.
kept up heavy strafing and ma
PAIN bombing of Wet Mini
troops at various points in Indo-
China. but there was no word
OF other activity in Laos.


In the vital Red River delta.
the French-held bastion around
Hanoi. the French continued
their mop-up drive and reported
killing 80 rebels and capturing
Is.


The French admitted, too, that
one OF their patrols fell into a
big Wet Mimi ambush SIS miles
southeast of Hanoi and suffered

The Commissioners have made a sensible
decision regarding proposed legislation to deal
more effectively with the narcotics problem in
Washington. They have rejected the contro-
versial plan for needle law" but have ap-
proved in principle the widely Endorsed idea of
compulsory disqualification for drug addicts
Federal and local authorities believe that a law
requiring disqualification of addicts will strike
body blow to the dope racket in this area.


The proposal for law outlawing "unauthor-
lied" use of hypodermic needles had the COM
mendable objective of making it difficult for
addicts to use narcotics by the injection method
Enforcement of such law would have been
difficult however. And the restriction might
have proved annoying and embarrassing to dia-
betics, who frequently carry hypodermic needles
with them for administration of inSulin
Furthermore, the needle program would not have
worried addicts who use narcotics by mouth or
who smoke opium or marihuana.


Much more practical and promising is the
plan for committing addictS to hospitals for
treatment, thereby removing them from the Gus
toners lists of the dope peddlers. The two
Federal narcotics hospitals have had consider
able success in curing and rehabilitating victims
of the drug habit. Compulsory disqualification
of addicts thus is humanitarian move in adj
dition to being crime deterrent. While the
District now lacks facilities for such treatment
the Public Health Service has indicated it's will
ingness to accept any addicts sent to the Fed
eral institutions by the District. That is for
tunate arrangement that should help to expedite
congressional approval of District hospitaliza-
ton program.

NEW YORK. July 15.-
Demand for steel is holding up,
the Iron Age, national metal
working weekly, said today. And
consumers are still anxious to
buy more steel than can be
delivered at regular mill prices.
| I'm the past several years the
experts have repeatedly under
estimated demand for STEEL"
Iron Age said. This time even
steel officials are not predicting
an early decline in demand.
Why? They can look at their
order books. they are within tele-
phone reach of purchasing
agents, they have just raised
prices without much squawk
from customers. and they do
have to buy scrap"


Scrap Prices Gain.


The weekly listed two major
reasons why the steel market,
though easing, is still long way
from saturation":


Steel scrap prices have risen
for the eighth consecutive week.
They usually reflect market pros
poets.


Major steel consuming indus
tries "are still going great guns.
Their purchasing agents will buy
if the price IS right"


Purchasing agents, it was
noted, don't want to be- stuck"
with high cost material that will
make them look bad when the
market turns softer. This, said
the magazine. is bad news to
converters, brokers and import
ers Of foreign STEEL" but "it
doesn't mean that demand has
lost its zip. There's still plenty
OF business on mill books. Order
backlogS are not appreclably
smaller than they were several
months ago. Fourth quarter
books just opened are filling at
a highly satisfactory pace"


No Lack of Orders.


Iron Age emphasized that al
though steel is still being sold at
premium prices by high-cost pro-
ducers, consumers will not paw
premiums when material becomes
abundant at regular prices.
Premium producers know this.
and they'll price their products
competitively when order books
grow thin" Cancellations, the
article added, are nowhere near
epidemic proportions" and the
steel made available has been
quickly gobbled up by other
customers"


The decline in production in
the past few weeks reflects va
cations. maintenance and hot
weather. along with some easing
OF the extreme pressure" on the
mills, but it is not due to lack
OF business, Iron Age declared.


While the ingot rate may limp
along at about 96 per cent of
capacity for the rest of this
month, it is expected to bounce
back to 100 per cent before long:
it may then stay there for a
number Of weeks before declin-
Ing moderately toward the end
OF the year. the magazine added.

much success. Next year the
MiddieS probably will play Will
liam and Mary, Dartmouth,
Stanford. Pittsburgh, Pennsyl-

The damaging effect Of grad
ing fills around trees in new
home developments is showing
up this spring in some areas.


The trees were healthy. many
of them mature, when the
houses were built a few years
ago. Even last year they looked
nice. Many of them are deteri-
Grating with startling sudden-
ness, according to tree experts.


It's most noticeable on naples,
oaks, dogwoods, hickories and
blrches. Leaves are smaller than
normal, and not such a deep
green. Twig dieback is quite
evident. Larger branches are
dying. Numerous suckers ap-
pear on the trunk.


Prompt corrective action must
be taken before these trees coll
lapse. Normally the trunk of an
established tree should flange
out just before it enters the soil
line. Where excessive fill has
been used-even two or three
inches of fine loan or clay are
harmful-the trunk enters the
soil in a straight line, like a
planted telegraph pole.


Excessive fill disturbs the re-
lationship between the root sys-
tenn and the air and water in
the soil. The roots need oxygen
just as leaves do, and altering
the water table is equally as
deleterious.


If trees are being suffocated
by fill, dig crowbar holes two
inches in diameter around the
root area. Fill these with sand
and charcoal. The sand permits
needed aeration. Charcoal abb
serbs toxic methane gases that
have been built up by the fill
and unable to escape.


Then feed the trees literally
to, promote better root develop
ment.


Trees that suffer from excess
sive fill more than three years
usually cannot be restored to
health. Once they deteriorate.
the end comes quickly. Elms.
poplars and willows will, how
ever, make the adjustment bet
ter than naples and oaks.

LONDON, July 22.-Scotland
Yard detectives picked up the
trail today of the men who cut
the telephone lines in the great
horse race betting coup last
Thursday and there were indica-
tions the law was about to close
in on the plotters.


Signs developed, too. that the
investigation has spread to the
continent, with French police
working to untangle some of the
strands.


The big break in the million
dollar coup came when police re-
ceived a tip on the cable SnipG
pers from a farmers wife, Mrs.
Eileen Perry of Heather Grange.


The exact number of persons
involved isn't known. There is
one theory, however. that the
ringleaders included three men
in Britain, two accomplices in
France and sixth man acting
as liaison between them.


List of IL Reported.


London's Evening Standard
said Detective Superintendent
Reginald Spooner had list OF
IL. names, "all we'll known in
horse racing circles"


Scotland Yard was silent on
progress of the investigation. The
coup worked this way:


A horse listed as Francasal-
a French trained two-year-old
with an undistinguished record
-romped home the winner of
the 2 o'clock race at Bath at 10
to-1 odds.


British bookies got a heavy
play on the horse shortly be-
fore the race started. They tried
to call the track to lay off some
of the bets. which are legal with
bookies in Britain, but found
the telephone cable cut. Had the
call gone through, the price
would have been hammered
down.


1t became a general assump-
t1on that ringer won the race.
At first it was believed Santa
Amaro, also French trained, had
been substituted for Francasal.
Some now believe Santa Amaro
was a decoy and that still a
third horse was involved. One
bettor who had seen both Fran
casal and Santa Amaro said:


Saw 3 Men Examine Cable.


I don't reckon they would
have substituted Santa Amaro.
If anything, that turkey is worse
than FrancaSal."


Both horses are under police
guard at EPSON race track.


Mrs. Perry said she saw a sleek
car draw up to the spot where
the cable was cut three weeks
ago. 1nfee Sporty-lOoklng types
got out. she said. and walked
into her husbands field which
lies behind a high hedge. The
cable runs over the hedge.


She said she watched the men
for 20 minutes, during which
time they examined the cable,
then drove away. Mrs. Perry
remembered the three index
letters of the cars license plate,
but couldn't recall the numbers.
Police have checked about 1000
plates without result.


Many of the bookies are still
holding the bets waiting for the
police to solve the case.

Queen Mary played important parts In six

English princess in the modern era Edward
VII admired and favored her, and his second
son. George v married her for love, not merely
for convenience. The influence she exerted

and George VI is matter of history with which
living generations are familiar. She was the
mentor of Elizabeth II when the present
sovereign was a child.


OF course, her position in the royal Victim
Windsor family accounted for some obvious
aspects of Marys impact on her times. Destiny
gave her vital place. If any woman ever
was Intended to be a regal wife and mother,
she was that woman. But accident does not
explain her remarkable success. She was a
symbol OF the best values of the distah side

passionate devotion to both her country and
the empire, her faithful obedience to consti-
tutional principles, her honorable pride, her
natural and instructive modeSty, her THOUGHT
fulness of others, her kindliness-these were
qualities which Lord Rosebery must have had
in mind when he referred to her as the "titular
and cherished head of the womanhood of
England" From such virtues her undoubted
pOWcI Was QeFlVeQ.


Mary herself was an heir to the throne

uaerely queen consort. When fate denied her
the highest place, she accepted a secondary
status with Smile-and made it in every
effective sense an imperial, even world asset
Through two global wars and through their
revolutionary aftermath, her counsel, her
advice, her guidance were constructive forces
She had many sorrows, many losses, she sur
Vived to see the British overseas realm crumble;
she witnessed in her old age the development
Of militant international communism, threat
ening everything she held dear.s y.....


But up to the last Mary was a defiance
Of disaster. The lines in her face grew hard
and. stern as she watched the increasing
turmoil and confusion, yet her eyes remained
bright and clear In her final photographs
her spirit still showed valiant resistance She
never ceased to be g. courageous personality.
In death she continues to have Importance
Her example will remain a power for which
millions everywhere should be grateful. Presi-
dent Eisenhower spoke for the entire American
community when he said "Queen Mary was
good and great Queen. Free people the world
over will mourn her loss"

Patagonian Darwin Rhea.


The zoo has two Darwin Rheas
the only ones in this country.

PARIS, Aug. 26. - France
struggled back to normal today
after almost three weeks of dis
location because of strikes. The
general back-to-work movement
encountered only a few islands
of resistance.


Railway trains were running
again. Paris buses and subways
were back on schedule. Big bun
dies of mail were being delivered
after the long tieup. Telephone
calls could be placed to most
parts Of France, although traffic
was much heavier than normal
and delays sometimes were long.


The two biggest holdout in
duStries were the nationalized
gas and electricity works and
coal mines. Even here, there was
some improvement. Gas and
electricity were supplied through
out the strikes except for minor
disruptions. In some provincial
towns, the regular workers were
reporting back today.


The coal mines in Eastern
France were starting up again
with almost a full complement
of workers, but there was little
activity in the big northern
basin, the most important in
France. Sufficient reserves of
coal are available to avoid any
pinch from a continuing strike.


The strikes, which at one time
had about 4 million persons off
the job, developed as a protest
to proposed economy DEGREES af-
fecting workers in government
run industries. Premier Joseph
Laniel's government has not an
nounced it's final decision on the
DEGREES.

REGGIO CALABRIA, Italy,
Oct. 23.-ReScue workers
searched today through wrecked
homes in a dozen small villages
of this Southern italian province
for victims of devastating flash
floods that may have claimed as
many as 100 lives.


Torrential rains continued to
pour on the stricken area from
Reggie Calabria along the Ionian
Sea this morning. They stopped
abruptly at noon. but heavy gray
clouds still hung over the area,
threatening new downpours.


In the Reggie Calabria area
alone SO dead have been &C
counted for. Scores are missing.


Worst Since 1908 Quake.


Hundreds were injured in the
disaster, the worst here since an
earthquake leveled the region in
1908. Residents said the dam
age, estimated in the billions of
lire, was far greater than that
caused by similar innundations
two years ago.


The floods struck without
warning just before dawn yester-
day, catching many persons
asleep in their beds. They were
preceded by IL hours of heavy
rains that turned large areas
into seas of mud, but caused only
minor damage.


Then suddenly. tremendous
cloudbursts struck mountains
only a few miles from the coast.
Water went racing toward the
sea through steep gullies that
are usually dry at this season.


Some of the torrents ripped
away bridges that usually are
5 to 10 yards above the river
beds. The boiling water Surged
out of the river courses, wreck
ing homes. tearing down COM
munications and power lines and
devastating thousands of acres
of vineyard and olive orchards.


The flood cut the Ionic high
way along the coastline in scores
of places and washed away many
secondary roads.


In San Gregorio near Reggie
eight bodies, including those of
three small children, were re-
covered from wrecked dwellings.
At Caracinello at least ii per-
sons died.


Priest Dies in Rescue.


Among II known dead in the
village of Oliveto was the parish
priest, Don Giuseppe Maesano,
who drowned trying to rescue a
drowning child.


The floods subsidized almost as
fast as they struck, but the wild
rain continued until noon, max
ing rescue work almost impos-
sible and dangerously under
mining hundreds of shaky homes.


italian soldiers. f1remen and
volunteers, including some
women. searched for the missing
and helped clear the debris clut-
tering village streets and high
ways.


Units of the italian Navy
steamed into Reggie today to
bring supplies to the stricken
population.
headline:

As Flash Floods Hit
Southern Italy Area

The recent exchange of military visits be-
tween Turkey, Greece and Yugoslavia offers hope
that these three Balkan powers may soon work
out mutual defense alliance. While reports that
such an agreement already is at an advanced
stage have been termed premature there have
been complimentary references from all three
capitals to the receptions accorded their military
missions in the other countries.


The round of visits began about two months
ago when Yugoslav group visited Greece and
Turkey. A Greek mission made the tour IN
November and Turkish mission has been in
Yugoslava since then. A further sign of entente
cordiale was given recently when Belgrade and
Athens raised their respective diplomatic mis-
sions from ministerial to ambassadoral status.


Each of the three powers borders on the
Iron Curtain; each faces the common threat OF
Soviet aggression. Forming an arc across Asia
Minor and the Balkans, the three countries offer
q barrier-or an avenue-for Russian penetra-
ton toward the Mediterranean or the Adriatlc
Seas. Greece and Turkey are now members OF
the NATO while Yugoslavia is receiving military
assistance from the West. Estimates of troop
strength credit Turkey with about 100000 under
arms, Yugoslavia with 100000 and Greece with
about 100000.


Deeply rooted political and economic diff
ferences historically have been disrupting IN
Balkan relations. Their reconciliation is not an
easy problem even in the common defense but
the temper being displayed currently in the
three capitals indicates that serious effort Is
being made to settle upon an amicable under
standing This much is progress and the effort
deserves Western Endorsement.
headline: CordioIity in the Balkans

SAIGON, Indo- China, May IL.
Laos Joined Wet Nam today in
protesting French devaluation of
the plaster. Wet Nam sources
predicted it would Skyrocket
prices 80 or 40 per cent and cause
grave internal difficulties.


Both Laos and Wet Nam de-
clared France had not consulted
with them prior to yesterdays
action reducing the value of the
1ndo- Chinese plaster from II
francs (4.9 cents) to 10 francs
20 centS). France took the step
to smash a black market cur
rency racket involving piasters.
francs and dollars which cost
France an estimated $3.50 mil
lion year.


A government spokesman in
Paris said all three Indo- Chinese
states had been informed of the
contemplated step. Cambodia is
the third state.


Wet Nam Premier Nguyen Van
Tam said the first result of the
devaluation would be an imme-
diate rising of prices.


Saigon Shaken and Angry.


Special police patrols were or
ganized to cope with any violence
in Saigon, shaken and angry
over the devaluation.


An immediate reaction was on
the black market, where the dol
lar rate shot to one for 80 piaS-
ters, compared with the legal
rate of one for 20 and the pre-
devaluation rate of one for so.


A communique from lie Van
Hoach. minister of information.
denied the decision had been
taken after consultation with the
Wet Nam government.


Premier Tam said he had
rushed an official complaint to
Jean Letourneau, French resi-
dent minister.


Premier Tam said the devalua-
tion step would stop the money
black market only temporarily
for before long the real value
of the plaster will fall to four
or five francs and that will open
the way to new possibilities for
trafflcking"


Air of Panic Prevails.


There was an air of panic in
business and commercial circles
here today, with little or no
transactions being made. Police
cracked down on at least two
food stores, one of which re-
bused to sell anything. The other
had raised its prices 20 per cent.


Premier Tam said the Wet
Nam authorities would inventory
food stocks and make an effort
to keep price rises within bounds,
for if prices get out of hand the
consequences will be disastrous
and will serve the interests of
Wet Mimi propaganda"


The French government said
the devaluation had been carried
out under the Pau treaty with
the Associated Indo- Chinese
States - Wet Nam, Laos and
Cambodia. This permits France
to modify the current fate after
consultation with the three
states. The French said they
had contacted the native gov
ernments shortly before the de-
ciSion was made. Obviously,
Premier Tam thought the notice
had been too short.


Fabulous Profits Made.


The wide difference between
the previous official value of the
plaster and its worth of eight
francs on the black market has
allowed many persons to make
fabulous profits through cur
rency purchases and transfers to
France


Critics charged that many of
the funds smuggled in found
their way into hands of the
Communicated Wet Mimi rebels,
who purchased arms for their
fight against the French.


The French expected the de-
valuation to cut the cost to them
of their war in Indo-China.

Want something new for din
ner? Try Don Carlos Onions
why the name I don't know. ex-

Peel 8 medium size onions, cut
a slice off the top and parboil for
10 minutes in salted water. Then
plunge them into cold water for
a minute. Scoop out the insides.
leaving fairly thick shells. Save
the pulp you've removed.


Now bake the shells in the
oven with a cup Of soup stock or
broth for an hour, basting them
often. Boil and mash 6 medium
potatoes and season them with
salt, pepper, butter and "a cup Of
milk. Whip them to fluffiness.
Stuff the onion shells with the
potatoes, and top with the
chopped onions from the inside
of the shells, after they have
been fried in butter. Reheat the
stuffed onions and serve.

PARIS, Aug. 1.-THE French
had only a few provincial news
papers and the English-language
European edition of the New
York Herald Tribune in which
to read today about the nations
continuing crippling strikes.


Most newspaper workers joined
for one day in the walkout in
state-run communications and
transport fields. Some out-of-
town papers published under an
agreement with the unions
which called for them to lay off
tomorrow instead of today. The
Herald Tribune was exempted
from the stoppage.


No Evidence of Break.


There was no evidence Of a
break in the strikes by govern
ment workers. Railroads were
still practically paralyzed. The
postal, telegraph and telephone
closure went into it's twelfth day.
Coal mines remained shut.


Premier Joseph Laniel and his
top ministers met yesterday to
discuss suggestions by Leon Jou-
haux, head of the Socialist trade
unions, for breaking the impasse.
Later they handed the labor
leader a reply but its nature was
not disclosed.


Labor Chiefs Meet.


A group of labor chiefs met
last night to study the govern
ment reply but gave no indica-
ton they were about to end the
strikes.


Paris bus and subway workers
voted today to stay out another
"a hours. Army trucks were try
ing to replace the city's usual
transportation.


Some independent union work.
ers and supervisors ran trains
on some lines, but members of
the two biggest unions were hav-
ing no part of it. The few over
crowded trains ran far behind
schedule.

KINGSTON, Jamaica -. (ANP)
- Queen Elizabeth, and her con-
sort, Prince Phillip, Duke of
Edinburg, will visit Jamaica Nov.
IS, this year. They will stay in
the island for two days before
proceeding on their Common
wealth tour across the Pacific TO
New Zealand and Australia.


Along with her Consort, the
Queen will fly from London and
land at Montego Bays airport on
the same spot of earth on this
far flung speck of the Empire
that Winston Churchill trod when
he stepped out of Harry Tru-
mans private plane, "The indie
pendence," several weeks ago.


Landing at sunrise in the
morning, the party will glimpse
the dazzling scenery of the beau
tifully enchanting north-coast of
sapphire-shaded sky and sea.


A close Gordon of frenized
Scotland Yard sleuths, bayonet-
brandishing and pistol buckling
policemen of Jamaica, along with
wily-eyed Criminal Investigation
Department officers, will ring the
Queen wherever she goes.


Leaving the airport amidst
heavily armoured guard, the dis
tinguished visitors will motor
across the palm-flecked fields of
Jamaica's tropic countryside, over
to Kings House where they will
stay with Gov. Hugh Macintosh
Foot, and his wife, Sylvia.


The government of Jamaica is
working out details of the visit
and will go to all extremes to
make their stay warmly comfor-
table.
headline: Queen Elizabeth To Visit Jamaica

months ago, the New Jersey State

BERLIN, July 4. - Rioters
against Red rule were reported
today to have blown up II Rus
sian tanks in Poland and other
tanks and factories were re-
ported sabotaged by blasting
and fire in rebellious East Ger
many.


The reports came from refu-
gees fleeing from the Commu-
mist East.


They told stories of continu-
ing sabotage after the June II
East German uprising, and said
large groups of Polish workers,
students and soldiers have been
in revolt since June 20.


The Polish incidents were re-
ported by the Sunday Telegraf
of West Berlin.


It said martial law has been
declared in the Silesian industrial
area of Poland and in Warsaw
and CrakoW.


Russian Troops Rushed Up.


Russian troops have been
rushed from East Germany into
Western Poland in efforts to sup
press the revolt, the Telegraf
said.


workers have been on strike
since June % in the entire Sile-
sian industrial area, principally
in Beuthen, GleiWitz, KattoWitZ,
Breslau, Koenigshuette, Dabrova,
Gornica. Rybnik. Tarnowitz and
Ratibor," the Telegraf said.


In huge demonstrations they
demanded the resignation of the
Communist government.


The militia either does not
interfere or else supports the
demonstrators. Polish partisans
have carried out large-scale ac-
tions. Near Koenigshuette they
destroyed II Soviet tanks. A
small Soviet infantry unit was
destroyed. The gas line between
Waldenburg and Goerlitz was
broken in six places.


The Soviet commander of the
Polish army, Marshal Konstantin
RokosSovsky, has declared mar
tial law in the Silesian industrial
area and in the areas of Warsaw
and Crakow"


Swelled to General Uprising.


The Telegraf said the disorders
began in some Polish areas on
June 20, in sympathy with the
East German rebellion. 1t re-
portedly grew rapidly and had
swelled to a general uprising in
Western Poland by June %


On that date. 10000 people
demonstrated at CrakoW's city
hall and 1900 students in front
of the University demanding the
government surrender, the
newspaper said.


The next day, June 80, mobs
stormed the CrakoW city hall
and its prison, the Telegraf said.


It claimed several Communist
prosecutors and four prison war
dens were hanged; the mobs set
up their own peoples court"
and threw 180 Communist party
and state officials into prison.


The next day, said the United
States State Department news
paper in Berlin, Die Neu Zeitung.
Russian tanks which had been
enforcing martial law in East
Berlin were ordered to the Polish
border.


No Official Confirmation.


There was no confirmation
from Western Allied authorities
of the Telegraf's account of a
widespread Polish revolt.


One West Berlin German who
has close contacts with Eastern
underground circles said he had
reliable reports that Polish
partisans had increased their
raiding and sabotage activities

BUENOS AIRES, Argentina,
May 9.-Argentine newspapers
cracked down further on United
States news agencies today under
pressure from the government of
President Juan D. Peron.


Dispatches from the Associ-
ated Press, United Press and
International News Service all
but disappeared from the pages
of newspapers.


At Gen. Peron's request, the
PeroniSta dominated Congress
yesterday ordered an investiga-
tion into foreign news agencies.
Gen. Peron accused agencies of
conducting an organized cam
paign abroad to defame him and
of taking orders from the United
States State Department.


Pro-government newspapers,
which represent the vast bulk
of the Argentine press, immedi-
ately made United States agency
dispatches conspicuous by their
absence. The big independent
newspaper La Nacion discon-
tinued publication of AP news
two days ago, the first such in
terruption in 35 years. La Nacion
also stopped publishing special
dispatches received nightly by
radio from the New York Times.
The Times and its BuenoS Aires
correspondent Edward A. Muir
row have been under editorial
attack.


The first direct official action
against a United States agency
came last night when the Min
istry of Communications ordered
the United Press to suspend its
distribution of dispatches to
newspapers in Argentina outside
Buenos Aires next Saturday. The
agency has been distributing its
dispatches in the interior through
the radio facilities of the Argen-
tine post Office. Thomas r. Cur
ran, UP vice president for Latin
America said this would cut of
news distribution to Is interior
newspapers.


Previously, two Buenos Aires
afternoon newspapers and eight
in the interior suspended publi-
cation of UP service after Gen.
Peron's attack on United States
agencies last week.

The Districts High School
Cadet Corps will march in the
inaugural parade, but a uniform
problem is complicating things.


Col. William E. Barkman, pro-
fessor Of military science and
tactics in the white schools. dis
closed today that a lack of ira
ditional blue uniforms will limit
most white schools to token rep
resentation.


Most white units now wear
cheaper khaki, but marchers are
being required to wear blues. A
few cadets still having blue uni
forms will represent the khaki
wearing units, Col. Barkman
said.


Anacostia High School, which
still wears blues, will have the
biggest contingent. Eastern prob
ably will have the smallest
only half a dozen marchers.


Proud Western, winner of
many drill competitions, expects
to send a somewhat better num-
ber-perhaps so. But Bell and
Chamberlain Vocational Schools
may not march at all.


Colored schools, which still
wear blues. will have about
equally divided representation
among them.


About a fourth of the 3,200-
man corps is scheduled to march.
The marchers will be formed
into four composite battalions,
two from the white schools and
two from the colored.


The 71-year-old corps has
taken part in almost every in
auguration since it's founding in
1882. The first was that of
President Grover Cleveland in
1885. The entire corps often
marched in earlier years.


There will be an innovation
this year, also along the uniform
line. White cadets are sched-
uled to wear Marine overcoats-
the first time overcoats ever have
been used by parading cadets.
The coats. Government surplus.
were bought by the schools for 81
apiece last year and are being
loaned or rented to cadets this
winter.


Colored cadets plan to march
without coats, however, accord
ing to Maj. Benjamin Hunton.
their instructor.


Col. Barkman marched in
Woodrow Wilson's inaugural
parade in 1918. when he was a
cadet at Eastern High School.
He expects to march with his
battalions Tuesday.


There's one possible hitch.
The corps won't march if the
weather is very bad, Col. Bark
man said. He and Maj. Hunton
will make the last-minute deci-
sion Tuesday morning.


The boys won't carry rifles.
Transporting the weapons to and
from school armories is too
complicated, Col. Barkman
explained.

The hospital ship Haven sailed
today for San Francisco with

servicemen freed from Com
munist prison camps in the past
two weeks.

Yokosuka. Japan, to take aboard
more patients. Unless there is
an unexpected delay, the great
white ship will dock in San
Francisco September IA.


CreWmen aboard the Haven
said they expect to pick up some
sick Americans who were re-
patriated from North Korean
camps and flown to hospitals
in Japan. They expect most
patients who board in Japan to
be i'll servicemen from units in
Korea and Japan. however.


Some of the 104 repatriates
aboard the Haven have been
waiting to sail since August 4,
when the exchange of prisoners
began.


Only trickle of less seriously
i'll repatriates arrived on the
Haven by helicopter from Pan
munjom. The more seriously
i'll were flown to Japan. Two
troop ships carrying able-bodied
repatriates are already approach
ing the West Coast.


A doctor aboard the Haven
this morning said most of the
patients aboard were suffering
from tuberculosis and malnutri-
ton,

MIAMI BEACH, Fla. The
strengthening spring season
at Miami Beach is more pro-
nounced than ever this year as
winter vacationers, reluctant to
leave the mild climate and
pleasant outdoors, are prolong-
ing their stays in the sun.


Reduced hotel and apartment
rates, now nearing the summer
lows that start May l. add an
economic incentive that many
are taking advantage of. It is
Miami Beach's boast that few
places in the world can even
come close to matching the lux
urious accommodations at late
spring and summer prices.


Miles of smooth, sandy beaches
some within the grounds OF
ocean-front hotels, others re-
served in municipal parks, invite
daily relaxation beneath the
palms. Cabana colonies, with
their atmosphere of informal
comfort, lure visitors for day.
long lounging.


Vacationers who like to fish
find this season one of the best
of the whole year. Tarpon are
here now on their annual spring
migration, and night the favor
ite time of many fishermen for
going after them.


Favorites such as the sailfish
marlin, bonefish, permit, snook
and channel bass remain in Mi
ami Beach waters the year
round. as do some trapon. Scores
of deep-Sea- cabin cruisers are
available for charter into the
Gulf Stream, while smaller craft
usually are used for bay fishing.
Some sport, chiefly with pan fish,
is to be had from bridges and
causeways.


Hundreds of hotels, apartment
buildings, restaurants and shops
provide a wide selection for the
visitor. Many vacationers drive
their own automobiles here while
others rent cars after arrival.

DOWLING and ice-skatng used to have
- nothing in common, but they do now. The
two sports have been put together to form
new game. with added appeal for fresh-air fiends
since it's played on outdoor Ice


Using standard duckpins and balls, outdoor
bowling -on-skates follows the same rules as
indoor bowling -on-foot. Two-by-four boards,
frozen firmly into the ice act as alley Sides and
foul lines and pin markers are painted on in
black. Players fall back from the foul line, take
a skating instead of running start, and toss
the ball down the frozen alley. The firm, smooth
ice acts much like hardwood floor, and with
practice, bowlers are able to achieve accuracy
and even attempt some of the tricky shots popu-
lar in indoor alleys. Padded canvas, stretched
tight behind the alleys, makes an easy backstop.


Estelle Dru, professional figure skater, and
the other lovely lassieS who tested out the new
sport at GroSsinger, N. Y- agreed with Sports
Director Irving Jaffee that the game should be
big attraction next year. Besides helping the
ladies keep in trim, the new sport is expected
to help novice skaters because they'll concen-
trate on bowling and lose their fear of falling
which is, according to Jaffee, the main obstacle
for beginners.

PARIS, Aug. 22.-French rail-

services remained strikebound
today despite a government set
tlement with two big non-Com-
munist unions. The wave OF
walkouts that have disrupted the
nations economic life for II
days appeared far from over.


The day even brought one new
tie-up. Paris bread bakers
walked out for three days, stiff
blow to citizens still unable to
telephone vacationing families
and jolting around the city in
army trucks used to replace the
strikebound subways and buses.


The bakers are seeking a wage
increase and paid vacations.
They belong to the Communist
led General Confederation of
Labor. left out of the negotia-
tions with the government that
led to the announced settlement.


Strike Continuation Ordered.


The CGT last night ordered
members in the postal and tele-
phone service to continue their
strike and decided to prolong
the walkout of bus and subway
workers another "a hours. No
decisions were announced con-
corning the federation's con-
tinuing strike on the railroads.


The two n-Communist
unions-the Socialist Workers
Force (FO) and the Christian
(Catholic) Workers Federation
(CFTC)-have, ordered mem
bers employed in the postal,
telephone and telegraph services
to return to their jobs but they
apparently were not being gen.
orally obeyed.


Letters still were not being
delivered and the telephone
service was still paralyzed. It
had been expected that the re-
turn of the two unions would
restore near-normal service since
they control the bulk of the
postal, telephone and telegraph
workers.


Set Off by Economy Plans.


The walkouts were touched off
by government economy plans
to trim public payrolls and lift
the retirement age of persons in
state-run services. Many Strik-
ers have added wage boosts to
their lists of demands.


In the case of the non-Com-
munist postal, telephone and
telegraph strikers, the govern
ment was reported to have
promised to:


/. Call into session before Sep
tember 80 a commission to con-
slider a general upward revision
of French wages.

strikers.

SEOUL. Sunday, Jan. 4.-Allied
light bombers hunted down Com
munist trucks and trains across
the snowclad waist of North Korea
last night and big B-29 superforts
slammed home bomb attacks on
two big Red supply centers.


The night raids came on the

Ground Fighting Lull.


Ground fighting slackened Sat-

frigid battle front.


An Eighth Army staff officer

Saturday and early Sunday in the
west. It was the first time in
more than a year, he said, that
the uneasy west had slumbered
through more than "a hours with
out artillery, mortar or small arms
duelS.


The Reds probed briefly in five
below zero weather last night at
four points along the central and
eastern fronts. None involved
more than 40 men. All were
turned back quickly.

main rail line between Sinanju

houses northeast of Sunchon, all
in northwest Korea.


The daylight attack Saturday
hit another supply center near
Sunchon, 80 miles northeast of
the Red Korean capital of Pyon-
gyang.

wings first plastered the Sunchon
supply. area with high explosive
bombs. Then they roared in low
on deadly strafing runs with
machine guns blazing. 1t was one
of the larger mass strikes of recent
weeks.

occupied buildings were totally
wrecked and others severely dam
aged. Pilots reported at least one
secondary explosion indicating hits
on ammunition or fuel stores.

half dozen different places.

PARIS, Aug. 8.-France today
floundered through a continued
strike in government-owned
public services which stranded
hundreds of American, British
and other foreign tourists in
Paris and other vacation spots.


Many of the workers who
walked out yesterday were back
on the job today, but the biggest
headache was in the railroads,
where operations were still spas
modic.


Uncertainty was so great that
sleeping car reservations were
refused. and the railway ticket
Offices frankly said they had no
idea whether any given train
would move.


1--WE just can't find out which
trains will run or how far they'll
get" one travel agent said. cts
still up in the air."


The American Express Co.
managed after an all-nlght
scramble to charter enough
buses to get 1872 passengers from
Paris to lie Havre for the sailing
today of the British liner Car
onia. The company was trying
to assemble another bus feet to
bring $50 passengers from Cher
bourg Monday. when another
British liner, the Queen Eliza
beth, will arrive from New York.


French officials said it was
difficult to say how many OF
yesterdays two million strikers
were still out but that. the figure
was over 100000.


The tourists woes stemmed
from an order of the Commu-
nist-run General Labor Fedora
ton (CGT) to drag yesterdays
24-hour railroad strike into to-
day. Thousands Of railroaders
obeyed, despite a call to end the
strike by Communist unions.


So far, Paris had no food
shortage, although fruits and
vegetables available at the CEN
trail market were 700 tons below
normal.


Coal Fields Closed.


A 24-hour mine strike almost
completely closed the nations
coal fields, with the walkout re-
ported 80 per cent effective.
Garbage collection was only
spotty in Paris, where many
municipal workers still stayed
off the job.


Funeral parlors opened, how
ever, and burial professions
were seen.


The four-day nationwide
postal, telegraph and telephone
strike continued, and the gov
renment announced plans for
using the army to collect letters
from TANNED mail boxes. This
it may do Monday.


Practically no hotel or travel
reservations to and from points
outside Paris could be made from
the capital because of the tele-
phone and telegraph strike.
Many of the comparatively few
travellers who managed to leave
Paris for other holiday points
went without knowing whether
they would find lodging on
arrival.


Airlines Operating
/ international airlmes were
operating without interruption
after the brief stoppage Of Air
France flights yesterday caused
by the walkout of ground crews
at Orly Airfield. Passenger ships
too, were coming and going
without difficulty from the main
ports, although some debarking
tourists were unable to proceed
very far beyond the docks.


The strikes among the public
services workers were touched of
by rumors, thus far unconflrmed
that Premier Joseph Laniel was
planning to save the government
some money at their expense
/ The rumors said that Mr.. Laniel
planned to increase the retire
ment age of civil servants from
81 to g., and dismiss thousands
of surplus government employees


The premier and his cabinet
early today completed DEGREES
which informants said might &c
into effect Monday. If these
DEGREES include the stern economy
measures the public workers
feared, strikes are expected to
be clamped down again in full,
force by Frances big unions.

non, who assigned special de-
tails to the case, has said the
homber's tactics "just don't make
sense"

automobile. Police who arrived

but they tended to cancel each other
out. Plus factors included mill and
export price fixing, short covering, re-

Worth street goods market.

holidays.

highways with mechanical and human wreck
age. The recorded tentative total Of 523 ex-
ceeded the estimate of the National Safety
Council, whose experts had warned that, unless
extraordinary care were exercised by all drivers,
about $40 persons would lose their lives during
the festive Christmas season. The traffic toll

545 for three-day holiday period, set in 1850.

some one else, during the traditional season of
peace and good will The statistics are especially

In approving a proposed toll road between
Richmond and Petersburg, Virginia'S State
Highway Commission has broken away from
a free-roads policy dating from the creation of
the commission in 1906. Whether the General
Assembly will go along with the commission in
this epochal change remains to be determined.
The toll road between the two cities will need
legislative authorization. Traditionally, how
ever, the Assembly has given great weight to
recommendations of the commission.


Before the automobile era toll roads were
numerous in Virginia and many other States.
Private companies were chartered to build and
operate the roads for public use-at price.
But the toll roads disappeared as motor traffic
grew and as the State launched comprehen-
Sive road construction and improvement pro-
gram Free roads were financed with revenues
from gasoline taxes and other assessments
against motor transportation. Virginia has
developed an excellent network of main high
ways and farm-to-market secondary roads
under this financing plan.


In recent years, however it has become
increasingly apparent that the demands OF
traffic we're outdiStancing the road extension
and Improvement work, which was limited by
tax revenues. Reluctance of the Legislature to
increase taxes has led to discussion of toll roads.
Half dozen other States meanwhile have had
impressive successes with the pay-as-you-go
turnpike plan. The past Legislature directed
six-man committee to make thorough study
of the toll plan and make recommendations to
the next Assembly. This committee is nearing
the end of its study The favorable attitude of
the highway commission on the Richmond
Petersburg toll project undoubtedly will infiu-
ence the committee in its recommendations.
The motoring publc's attitude also must be
considered. But the growing popularity of such
expressways as the Pennsylvania and New
Jersey turnpikeS indicates which way the winds
are blowing.

reached on the new proposal.

BERLIN. July 9.-The Com
munists lifted the iron curtain
before riot-torn East Berlin to-

travel into the Russian sector of
the divided city for the first

Frontier Patrols Doubled.


Though Red German infantry

Each automobile and truck at

Restoration of the normal in

secondary demand of the strik-
ers yesterday. The Reds an
nounced they would accede only
a few hours after the sitdowns
started. West Berlin's three al

token support for the satellite
governments declaration that its
police would maintain law and
order in East Berlin. The Rus
sian army had done this job since
it roared in three weeks ago to
smash the bloody uprising.


Lifting of the border blockade
today Cancelled the last of the
emergency restrictions in East
Berlin, but Maj. Gen. P. T. Di-
brova, the Red army comman-
dant, has not yet formally de-

killed in an accident. The COM
mittee confirmed reports that
Bonetto struck an electric light
post while his Lancia car was
racing through Silao.


Bonetto was fighting furiously
at the time to keep his lead over
Humberto Maglioli's Ferrari
Maglioli moved into the lead
when Bonetto failed to arrive at
Leon. finish line of the first of
the days two laps.


Bonetto, third in the Mile
Miglia race this year, had won
the first leg of the Pan-American
event Thursday. He was second
in both of yesterdays legs, but
was still in the lead in the gen.
eral classification.


He was the third Italian driver
killed during the three days OF
this event. Antonio Stagnoli and
his co-pilot, Giuseppi Scotuzzi
were killed the first day of the
race. Four spectators were also
killed the first day, making the
total deaths SO far seven.

SEOUL, Sunday, March g.
South Korean guns, firing
through a drizzling rain at Chi
nese Reds advancing in the mud,
smashed two Chinese Red COM
pany attacks yesterday on the
western front.


The futile assaults cost the
Reds 106 men dead or wounded
from a total attack force of
300 to $50 men, the 9th Army
estimated. {:


The Korean 155-mile battle
line was a dismal scene, blank
eted by the drizzle. Unseasonably
warm weather thawed snow
spots and made quagmires for
wallowing supply trucks.


The mist and low clouds
grounded all but weather re-
connaisSance planes, the 5th
Air Force reported.


Attackers Lose Spirit.


South Korean troops holding
an outpost near Kelly Hill on
the western front used big guns
and criss-crosS machinegun fire
to cut down the first Chinese
company attack before dawn
yesterday. The action lasted an
hour.


Another Red company attack
lacked spirit and was beaten off
in 80 minutes.


Several smaller Chinese at
tacks were repulsed in the Ku-
mhwa Ridge sector in central
Korea.


North of Kelly Hill. Chinese
Red artillery fired a two-hour
barrage of 2,100 shells at Allied
positions around Old Baldy,
southwest of Chorwon, shortly
after midnight Friday. The Red
guns blazed sporadically until
daylight yesterday.


Thaw Causes Trouble.


Associated Press Correspond
ent Forrest Edwards reported
from the eastern front that mild
spring temperatures. arriving
month early, we're causing trou-
BILE both for the foot soldier and
the supply truck.


Fighting men who have
grown used to wading through
snow are slipping, sliding and
falling in the two inches of
greasy clay mud that covers the
roads and cascades down ridge
lines into the Valleys" Mr.. Ed
wards said.


Ending a seven-day inspection
tour of air bases, Air Force Sec
retary Harold E. Talbot flew
eastward today toward Washing
ton, impressed with what he
saw. He said in Tokyo before
leaving that the Far East Air
Force was fully capable of cop
ing with the difficult task it
faces"

officials said lack of Coast

and although North American
crewmen helped save Lolita -
crewmen from drowning, the
Miss Thelma" was surrounded
by Mexican craft and herded

since.

Trabert and Vic Seixas struck

subduing Canada's Lorne Main
and Paul Wiley, 2-6. 6-3, 6-3,
GO, in a doubles match played
in blustery winds and steady
rain.


The triumph gave the United
States a 80 lead in the best
three five match series

of the final two singles tomorrow.


Trabert and Seixas figured in
the other two points also, scor-
ing straight-Set victories over
Henri Rochon and Lorne Main
in yesterdays opening singles.


Americans Not at Peak.


The new United States singles
champion and the Wimbledon
titleholder were something short
of overpowering in doubles, how
ever, and apparently will have to
do a lot of boning up before they
stand much chance against the
Australian tandem of Lewis Hoad
and Ken Rosewall.

Americans another trip to Aus
tralia where they must meet the
winner of match between Bel
GUM and India in the inter-
zone finals before they can chal-
lenge the Aussies for the big
international trophy.


Wiley Stars in First Set.


The Americans didn't work
we'll together in the first set and
frequently were caught fiat
footed on some sharp volleying
and overhead smashes by Wiley,
23-year-old freshman member of
the Canadian forces.


But after losing Seixas' service
in the fourth game of the open
ing set and ultimately the set.
the Americans smothered the
Canadians with their big serv-
ices. They didn't lose a delivery
once in the last three sets.


The match was played before
a crowd of some 900 hardies at
the Mount Royal Tennis Club.


Lawrence Baker, chairman of
the United States Davis Cup Sc
lection committee and non-play-
ing captain of the team in these
matches. said Seixas and Trabert

bitter Trieste dispute.


Belgrade threatened yester-
day-in its fourth protest in
three days-to rush its own
tough troops to the Italian bor-
der unless Italy halted pro
vocative" maneuvers there.


Rome replied last night that
Italian forces had taken only
precautionary and protective
measures"


With the final word thus far

old quarrel, Italy scoffed at
Yugoslovia's pretended frontier
incidents" Rome said even if
the incidents were true they
seemed "of very modest nature
for so much hullabaloo.
Now Free Territory.
The Adriatic frontier region,
long disputed between Italy and
Yugoslavia, is now an interna-
tional free territory divided into
two zones pending a settlement
of it's future. British and United
States troops occupy one section,
including the port, and Yugo-
slavia administers the other.
Exchanges between Italy and

grown more bitter in the last few
days despite expressions of con-
| fidence by leaders of both coun-
tries that the new f1areup would
not lead to anything critical.
Western diplomats have urged a
policy of calm.


Yugoslavia charged this week
that Italian engineers were dig
ging trenches and building pill
boxes along the border and Ital-
ian tanks were maSsing at Co
rita. The town is not far across

village of Okrajaglica, where

make a major speech tomorrow
Tito Move Feared.
/ Italian fears that Tito would
use the occasion to announce
annexation of the Yugoslav-
controlled zone of Trieste
touched off the latest angry con-
troversy.


Fresh fuel was added to the
growing blaze by United States
Secretary of State Dulles re-
marks Thursday on the Trieste
issue. He indicated the United
States might now consider al
ternatives to its 1948 stand that
the whole territory should be
returned to Italy.


Italy called the Dulles state
ment a betrayal.


The semiofficial YugoslaI
news agency Yugopress inter-
preted Mr.. Dulles words as as
surance that the Trieste ques-
tion would be settled in a way
favorable to Yugoslavia's vital
interests.

South Boston people associated
with the Red Cross are always
asked this question: How is the
blood program going?


Here is a progress report issued
this week by Gen. Daniel Need
ham, blood program chairman for
the Boston Metropolitan Chapter


Blood donations both in March
and April throughout the State
increased over any month during
the past IA months. In March
there were 1854 donations at
the Red Cross Blood Center, 314
Dartmouth st, Boston, and at
bloodmobile visits throughout the
State.


Because of these donations,
donors through the Red Cross
were able to help thousands of
people who needed lifeblood.
They included thousands of sick
and injured, who received this
blood without charge, in Greater
Boston and Massachusetts civil
ian hospitals, and others who lie
on sick beds in military and Vet
erans Administration hospitals in
the State.


Other blood donations were
sent to processing laboratories
under government contract where
plasma was fractionated into
serum albumin - used to fight
shock for soldiers in Korea - and
into gamma globulin which will
be used here this summer for
people exposed to gripping polio.


Gen. Needham said the State
Department of Public Health has
been named by the federal gov
ernment as the sole distributing
agency for gamma globulin.


Emphasizing that this blood de-
rivative will be in short supply,
the State Department of Public
Health announced that through
blood contributed to the Red
Cross there will be available
$500 vials of gamma globulin-
enough for 5000 children-for
Massachusetts, this summer.

lands, July 24.-The lower house
of the Dutch Parliament yester-
day overwhelmingly approved
the treaty setting up the Euro
pean Defense Community. The
United States has strongly sup
ported establishment of the EDO.


The vote was 75-11 with only
the Communists and extreme
right wing opposed to the treaty
which is intended to unite the
armed forces Of The Netherlands,
Belgium, Luxembourg, France,
Italy and West Germany for Eu-
ropean defense.


The Dutch upper house must
still vote on the draft and Queen
Juliana sign it before The Meth
erlands' ratification is complete.
This is expected in September


Only one country-West Ger
many-has already ratified the
treaty and even there it is being
fought before the Supreme Court
and may possibly be thrown out
on constitutional grounds.
headline:
Dutch Lower House Backs


European Defense Treaty.

The Air Force has announced
that pilot training will be opened
to civilian high school graduates
beginning November /. The
move is designed to stimulate
applications for flight training.


Heretofore civilians have had
to complete at least two years
of college before being eligible
for military pilot training. :


Enlisted airmen in the Air
Force have been eligible for pilot
training for two years. and last
August the Air Force made high
school graduates Of the avia-
ton cadet program eligible for
observer training on an expert
mental basis.


The Air Force said the lower
ing of formal education re-
quirements for plotting candi-
dates does not indicate =any
lowering of selection standards
since high school applicant must
pass the same qualifying tests
as those with two or more years
of college.


Civilian applicants who quail
fly for pilot training will be
authorized a four-month defer
ment from the draft pending
selection and assignment to
training, the Air Force said.

Gray wolves have been losing
ground for years. Once packs
numbered thousands. Today
authorities estimate there are
slightly over 1000, a danger
ously low figure if anything like
a serious disease attacked them.


They are restricted to the
northern extremes of Wisconsin,
Michigan and Minnesota. There
are large numbers in Alaska.
Canada and Mexico.


Hunters and cattlemen are not
in favor of protecting them.
Wildlife conservationiSts despair
of this attitude since it would
deprive us of authentic figures in
our wild animal group.


The number of practical work
ing sanctuaries is pitifully few
Lobo, the gray wolf, has very
few friends and fewer defenders.
Throughout history his principal
foe has been the owner of live
stock.


Gray wolves ask no quarter
and give none. He can and does
outsmart man and though the
dog is his direct deScendent, the
wolf makes short work of him.


The serious situation facing
the gray wolf was debated in
Congress. Federal funds were
provided to employ skilled hunt
ers and to pay scientists to
scheme for his defeat. Lobo
trotted merrily past poisoned
carcaSSes. baited, concealed
traps and hid from gunners, still
outsmarting his arch foe-man.


Much has been written about
the VOLTS devotion to his mate

The young remain with their
parents until establishing a
